1606.04474.tldr: The original proof that an optimization procedure can itself be learned. An LSTM is trained to act as an optimizer — ingesting gradients and emitting weight updates — by unrolling the optimizee's training.
results: The learned optimizer generalizes to optimizees, networks, and task distributions it was not trained on.
Recovered hand-designed behavior (momentum-style updates) without being told to.
limitations: Meta-trained on small, specific task distributions; scaling to large-scale training remained open (and largely still is).
1606.04474.fits: The conceptual root of the whole list: if the *improver* is learnable, then the improver can be improved. Everything from TextGrad to DGM is a descendant of this idea.
1606.04474.reading: Read §2–3 (the coordinatewise LSTM and how unrolling works); skim the transfer experiments.

2410.04444.tldr: The self-referential ideal made concrete with an LLM: the agent's behavior is code (prompts + tools) that it can inspect and rewrite, so no fixed, hand-designed optimizer sits in the loop.
results: The agent can modify its own logic and improve without a human-authored optimization routine.
Demonstrates self-reference and code-as-identity as an RSI substrate.
limitations: Self-modification is bounded and validated heuristically — no formal guarantees of goal preservation.
2410.04444.fits: The theory-side counterpart to the empirical Darwin Gödel Machine (stage 7). Read them as a pair: this is the 'what', DGM is the 'does it work'.
2410.04444.reading: Focus on how it frames self-reference (§3) and the self-modification loop; the paper is more a framework than a benchmark result.

2003.03384.tldr: Evolves complete ML algorithms — not just hyperparameters — from a tiny space of scalar/vector math operations, discovering update rules that work from scratch.
results: Rediscovered backpropagation and Adam-style momentum purely through evolution.
Evolved algorithms that generalize to held-out tasks, with minimal human bias in the search space.
limitations: Only tiny problems (small MLPs, toy datasets); doesn't scale to modern models.
2003.03384.fits: Pre-LLM 'AI designing AI'. The evolutionary-search machinery here is the direct ancestor of AlphaEvolve and MLEvolve (stage 9 / stage 8).
2003.03384.reading: Skim the search-space design (§3) and the discovered algorithms (§4); don't dwell on the experimental scale.

2310.03714.tldr: Reframes prompt engineering as program optimization: declare what each LM call does (a signature), then let a compiler optimize the prompts and few-shot demos inside against a metric.
results: GPT-3.5 + DSPy pipelines matched or beat hand-written GPT-4 prompts on several tasks.
The optimizer (bootstrapped demos or a prompted optimizer) is reusable across tasks.
limitations: Needs a well-defined automatic metric — the optimization is only as good as that signal.
Prompt/compile quality still depends on the underlying search or bootstrap strategy.
2310.03714.fits: The most *useful* artifact in the list: it's the mental model (separate structure from parameters) that harness-level RSI generalizes. Read before TextGrad.
2310.03714.reading: Read the signature/module abstractions (§2–3) and one optimizer (§4). Then actually try the library.

2406.07496.tldr: Generalizes backprop to text: treat every textual variable in a compound system as a parameter, and backpropagate natural-language criticism through the graph to update each one.
results: Optimizes prompts, code, and answers in one end-to-end loop.
Outperformed hand-crafted prompts and prior prompt optimizers across reasoning and coding benchmarks.
limitations: Textual 'gradients' can be noisy or uninformative; performance is still bounded by the base model's capability.
2406.07496.fits: The cleanest mental model of 'differentiating' an AI pipeline. Pair with DSPy: DSPy is structured program optimization, TextGrad is free-form textual backprop.
2406.07496.reading: Read the computation-graph formalism (§3) and the text-gradient update rule (§4).

2303.11366.tldr: Verbal reinforcement learning: when the agent fails, it writes a natural-language reflection on what went wrong, stores it in memory, and injects it into the next attempt — no weight updates.
results: 91% pass@1 on HumanEval with GPT-4, a large jump over the base model.
Improved on decision-making (AlfWorld) and sequential reasoning without any fine-tuning.
limitations: Improvement lives only in the context window — bounded and non-persistent across sessions.
Works best on episodic tasks with clear success/failure signals.
2303.11366.fits: The ancestor of nearly every 'memory agent' in stage 4 (ExpeL, A-MEM, EvolveR, …). Read it first and watch how each successor adds persistence or structure.
2303.11366.reading: Read §3 (the reflect→store→retry loop) and the HumanEval result. Short paper.

2305.16291.tldr: Lifelong skill acquisition in Minecraft: an automatic curriculum proposes tasks, execution-verified code skills accumulate in a library, and feedback refines them — all with a frozen GPT-4.
results: ~3.3× more unique items collected and key tech-tree milestones unlocked far faster than prior agents.
The skill library compounds: later tasks reuse and build on earlier verified skills.
limitations: Minecraft-specific and depends on a strong base model; skill code can still hallucinate and needs environment feedback to correct.
2305.16291.fits: The canonical *skill-library* paradigm. Its 'code-as-skill, verify-in-environment' loop is reused by DGM, AgentFactory, and the embodied self-improvement line.
2305.16291.reading: Read the three components (§3–4) and the automatic-curriculum mechanism; then run the repo (stage 10).

2510.04618.tldr: Treats an LLM's entire context as an evolving playbook of ID'd, helpful/harmful-counted bullets, self-improved by a Generator/Reflector/Curator loop applying structured incremental delta updates with deterministic non-LLM merging — fixing the brevity bias and context collapse of monolithic prompt rewriting.
2510.04618.method: Context is a structured playbook of itemized bullets, each with metadata (unique ID, helpful/harmful counters) and content (a strategy, concept, or failure mode). Three same-model roles (DeepSeek-V3.1 non-thinking throughout, to isolate context effects) loop: the Generator solves a query while flagging which bullets helped or misled; the Reflector diagnoses the trace — up to 5 refinement rounds — extracting key insights and tagging each bullet helpful/harmful/neutral; the Curator emits compact JSON delta operations (ADD-only in the shipped prompts, IDs system-assigned) merged by deterministic non-LLM logic, so deltas batch in parallel. Grow-and-refine controls growth: counters update in place and semantic-embedding dedup prunes redundancy, either proactively after each delta or lazily when the context window is exceeded. Offline mode runs up to 5 epochs over training queries (system prompts); online mode updates after each test sample (agent memory).
results: AppWorld (DeepSeek-V3.1, ReAct base avg 42.4): offline ACE 59.4 (+17.0) with GT labels, 57.2 (+14.8) without; beats ICL by 12.3 and GEPA by 11.9 offline, and Dynamic Cheatsheet by 7.6 online (online ACE 59.5, +17.1) — the headline +10.6% agent average.

AppWorld leaderboard (09/2025): 59.4% avg matches top-ranked IBM CUGA (60.3%, GPT-4.1-powered) using smaller open-source DeepSeek-V3.1; online ACE surpasses CUGA by 8.4% TGC / 0.7% SGC on test-challenge.

Finance (FiNER+Formula, base 69.1 avg): offline ACE with GT 81.9 (+12.8), beating ICL/MIPROv2/GEPA by 10.9 avg; DDXPlus medical 75.2→90.2 (+15.0, vs GEPA's 76.4); BIRD-SQL 47.8→52.9 (+5.1) — the headline +8.6% domain average.

Cost: vs GEPA offline AppWorld −82.3% latency (53,898→9,517s), −75.1% rollouts (1,434→357); vs DC online FiNER −91.5% latency (65,104→5,503s), −83.6% token cost ($17.7→$2.9); 86.9% average latency reduction; 91.8% cache hit rate cuts billed input cost 82.6%.

Ablation: removing incremental delta updates drops test-normal TGC 76.2→67.3 and SGC 64.3→46.4 (−11.7%/−27.8% relative); gains hold across GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, and Llama-3.3-70B without algorithm changes.
advantages: First to name and quantify context collapse — a Dynamic Cheatsheet rewrite on AppWorld shrank 18,282 tokens to 122 in one step, accuracy 66.7→57.1, below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline — and to fix it structurally via deterministic localized deltas rather than just scoring higher.

Self-supervised by construction: +14.8% on AppWorld offline with no GT labels, learning purely from execution feedback; the Reflector is separable and weak reflectors still gain (+5.9 with GPT-OSS-120B), with noise tolerated unless adversarial every single step.

The ADD-only, system-ID'd, helpful/harmful-counted bullet playbook merged by non-LLM code is directly portable discipline for any RSI harness with unboundedly growing notes — hyperparameters prove forgiving (dedup 50–90%, pruning trigger 10K–100K tokens, all stable).
Reframes long-context cost: richer playbooks don't scale billed cost linearly because KV/prompt caching amortizes reused context (91.8% of eval input tokens served from cache on GPT-5.1).
limitations: Feedback quality is load-bearing — the paper's own caveat: without GT labels or reliable execution signals, ACE degrades (FiNER online no-GT 67.3, −3.4) as spurious reflections pollute the playbook, and it drops below base under adversarial reflections every step (66.7 vs 70.7).

Relies on a reasonably strong Reflector: weak models show smaller gains (Llama-3.3-70B reflects noisily), and over-reflection hurts — 10 rounds degrade to 65.2 avg vs 67.6 at 5 ('overthinking' injects noisy updates).

Not for concise-context tasks: the paper concedes HotPotQA-style retrieval QA and fixed-strategy games like Game of 24 benefit more from terse instructions than comprehensive playbooks — detail-heavy domains are where it wins.
Context capacity is managed by dedup/pruning thresholds, not eliminated; leader-board comparison to IBM CUGA is explicitly a rough contextual reference, not a controlled baseline.
2510.04618.fits: Stage 4's context-as-evolving-artifact anchor: generalizes Dynamic Cheatsheet's test-time memory and GEPA's prompt evolution into structured playbook evolution with collapse resistance. The prompt-space complement to Voyager's code-skill library; its ADD-only delta discipline pairs with A-MEM's agentic memory organization.
2510.04618.reading: §2.2 for the collapse case study (Fig 2), §3.1–3.2 for delta updates and grow-and-refine, Tables 1–2, §4.6 + Appendix A.5 for the incremental-update ablation, Appendix C for ACE-vs-GEPA/DC mechanism contrasts.

2510.16079.tldr: EvolveR closes the experience loop inside RL training: the agent distills its own trajectories into guiding/cautionary principles kept in a scored, deduplicated, pruned base, retrieves them via a learned <search experience> action, and GRPO-trains on experience-conditioned rollouts — beating Search-R1 across seven QA benchmarks.
2510.16079.method: Three alternating phases (§3). (1) Offline self-distillation, policy frozen: the agent's own πθ reviews each trajectory under an expert persona and emits a principle — a natural-language description plus knowledge triples, typed 'guiding' (success) or 'cautionary' (failure). Same-problem candidates are pairwise-deduped by LLM votes; each survivor then passes a two-stage gate (BGE-M3 cosine retrieval + binary LLM equivalence check): add if max similarity < 0.85, else merge the source trajectory under the matched principle. Every principle carries a Laplace-smoothed trust score s(p)=(c_succ+1)/(c_use+2); scores below 0.3 are periodically pruned. (2) Online interaction: top-3 principles are retrieved on demand via a learned <search experience> action, alongside <search knowledge> document retrieval. (3) Policy evolution: GRPO (G=8 rollouts per prompt, 128 prompts/step) maximizes 1.0·exact-match + 0.1·format reward over experience-conditioned trajectories, after a ~700-sample GPT-4o cold-start SFT.
results: Seven QA benchmarks, EM: top average at both scales — 0.382 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 0.417 (7B) vs Search-R1 0.303 (base, 3B) / 0.385 (instruct, 7B); best in five of seven columns at 3B (NQ 0.434 vs 0.406, HotpotQA 0.373 vs 0.284, Bamboogle 0.328 vs 0.264), trailing Search-R1-base by 0.003 on TriviaQA (0.584 vs 0.587) and PopQA (0.434 vs 0.435).

Self- vs teacher-distillation reverses with scale (Table 2): GPT-4o-mini distillation wins at 0.5B (avg 0.220 vs 0.150) and 1.5B (0.290 vs 0.270), but self-distillation wins at 3B (0.382 vs 0.370) — the paper's 'cognitive alignment' claim.

Retrieval is load-bearing: the same trained weights denied the experience base at eval drop 0.382 → 0.340 (3B), 0.270 → 0.123 (1.5B), 0.150 → 0.078 (0.5B); swapping GRPO for SFT on the identical successful trajectories costs 0.382 → 0.357 (7% relative).

Quality control demonstrably works (manual audit of 100 principles): the high-score tier holds 82% ideal / 8% incorrect-misleading vs 26% / 24% in the low tier; the base grows to 49,934 principles with top-3 latency of 0.20 s and stable EM, peaking at 0.410 near 45k.

Scaling and learning dynamics: avg EM rises 0.150 (0.5B) → 0.270 (1.5B) → 0.382 (3B); principles distilled later score higher (interval-4 avg trust 0.500 vs 0.462 for interval 1), and pruning is threshold-robust (avg 0.265–0.276 for θprune ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9} on 1.5B).
advantages: Closes the loop inside RL rather than around a frozen model: distill every step (params frozen), retrieve during rollouts, GRPO over experience-conditioned trajectories — Reflexion/ExpeL/Memento never touch weights, Search-R1-style search RL has no experience channel. Component attribution: RL alone 0.325, retrieval without RL 0.357, full framework 0.382.

Memory with an audited trust ledger: the (c_succ+1)/(c_use+2) score decides survival (θprune = 0.3) and tracks human-judged quality (82% vs 26% ideal), robustly — performance moves only 0.265 → 0.276 across the whole θprune sweep.

Shows self-distillation can beat a stronger teacher at 3B: principles matched to the policy's own failure modes outperform GPT-4o-mini's, direct evidence against the external-scribing paradigm (ExpeL-style insights from a big model).
The experience base scales as an artifact: ~50k principles with 0.04–0.20 s top-3 retrieval (Milvus, BGE-M3) and no collapse under noise accumulation; full 3B lifecycle trains in ~39.4 h on 8×A100.
limitations: Scale-dependent distiller (paper's own finding): below 3B, self-distillation loses to GPT-4o-mini teacher distillation (0.5B avg 0.150 vs 0.220; 1.5B 0.270 vs 0.290); the conclusion concedes principle quality is 'inherently tied to the base model's capabilities'.

Capability is split between policy and base, not internalized: denying retrieval at eval costs 0.382 → 0.340 (3B) and 0.150 → 0.078 (0.5B), and the w/ exp-absorb attempt to learn from retrieved principle tokens degrades 0.382 → 0.371 (noisy top-k), left to future work.
Distillation failure mode is vagueness: low-score-tier principles are 50% vague and 24% incorrect/misleading (audit of just 100 samples) — scoring prunes but never eliminates bad advice.
Scope is QA-shaped: seven knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks with an exact-match headline; whether strategy principles transfer to non-QA agent domains is untested.
2510.16079.fits: Stage 4 (memory, reflection & skills): converts the Reflexion/ExpeL verbal-reflection loop into curated principles plus GRPO signal, closing experience → memory → weights end-to-end. Pairs with the EvolveR repo card (implementation detail), ACE (context-only evolution), A-MEM/MemoryBank (memory organization without RL), and Search-R1-lineage RL agents.
2510.16079.reading: §3.2 (distill/dedup/integrate, Eq. 1–2), §3.3 (reward + GRPO), §5.2–5.3 (Tables 2–7, the 100-principle audit), A.2.1/A.2.3 (SFT-vs-GRPO, learning dynamics), A.1 (hyperparameters).

2605.23904.tldr: Trains the skill document as the external state of a frozen agent, with a separate optimizer model making bounded add/delete/replace edits accepted only on held-out validation gain.
results: Improves across six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution harnesses.
Zero extra inference-time model calls at deployment — all optimization happens offline.
limitations: Bounded, acceptance-gated edits are deliberately conservative — the tradeoff is a slower skill-evolution rate.
2605.23904.fits: The 'treat the skill like a trained parameter' position — skill evolution with the discipline of weight-space optimization. Contrasts with free-form self-revision approaches.
2605.23904.reading: Read the textual-learning-rate / acceptance-gate design (§3–4) — that discipline is the reusable idea.

2408.08435.tldr: A meta-agent programs new agents: it proposes agent designs as executable code, evaluates them, and iterates — including a re-architect step that learns to improve the meta-agent's own prompt.
results: Discovered agents that outperform state-of-the-art hand-designed agents on coding, math, and QA benchmarks.
Agents transfer across models (e.g., discovered agents boost GPT-4 performance).
limitations: Search is compute-hungry (many LLM calls); the meta-agent itself is initially hand-designed.
2408.08435.fits: The harness-level flagship: the 'improver' is an agent generating executable improvements. Stage 5's anchor — most later harness-evolution work extends this loop.
2408.08435.reading: Read the meta-agent search + re-architect mechanism (§3) and the transfer results.

2310.02304.tldr: Bootstraps a recursive code improver from a seed: an LLM writes and improves a scaffolding program, and that generated program is itself an improver that can improve the code that improves it.
results: Improved over GPT-4 on GSM8K and WebShop, including the generated improver improving itself.
Demonstrates the improver-improves-the-improver loop on real code.
limitations: Recursive gains can plateau; depends on a strong seed model and self-improvement meta-prompt.
2310.02304.fits: The most literal 'recursive' demo — the scaffolding that does the improving is itself improved. A bridge between ADAS (search) and DGM (self-modification).
2310.02304.reading: Read the seed-improver construction and the meta-prompt (§3–4). Short paper.

2605.09998.tldr: Reset-free online self-improvement for embodied agents: the agent alternates between acting and refining its own prompt, sub-agents, skills, and memory within one continuous trajectory.
results: Originated from Gemini Plays Pokémon — the first system to complete Pokémon Blue/Yellow Legacy (hard mode) and Crystal without a lost battle.
Removes the human from the refinement loop, automating what was previously human-in-the-loop harness tuning.
limitations: Embodied/eval cost is high; single-trajectory online adaptation is complex to stabilize.
2605.09998.fits: The embodied, reset-free counterpart to prompt-optimization harnesses. Extends the loop toward model-weight co-learning — a bridge to SIA's joint updates.
2605.09998.reading: Read the act/refine alternation (§3) and the Pokémon results; note the contrast with reset-based prompt optimizers.

2605.27276.tldr: A Feedback-Agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) alternately rewrites a task agent's scaffold and RL-tunes its weights (LoRA on gpt-oss-120b), merging the harness-update and test-time-training silos into one loop that beats both single-lever variants on all three benchmarks.
2605.27276.method: Three LLM components: a Meta-Agent writes the initial scaffold A1 from the task spec and reference code; the task-specific agent (gpt-oss-120b) runs the benchmark in a sandbox (read-only data, private working dir); a Feedback-Agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) reads the full trajectory — every prompt, response, tool call, and extracted answer per instance, not summary metrics — plus the scaffold and scores, then picks the next step: a harness update (A_{g+1} = F(A_g, τ_g, E_g, U); weights frozen) or a weight update (LoRA r=32, lr 4e-5 on gpt-oss-120b, H100s via Modal; scaffold frozen). It also selects the RL algorithm from a six-entry menu (PPO+GAE, GRPO, entropic advantage weighting, REINFORCE+KL, best-of-N behavioral cloning, DPO) from reward structure; in practice scaffold iteration runs first, switching to weights when harness progress stalls. Gate: a deterministic per-instance verifier scores every step.
results: LawBench 191-class Chinese charge classification (top-1 accuracy, 913-item held-out test): 13.5% initial → 50.0% harness-only — the scaffold converged on a TF-IDF + LinearSVC pipeline, abandoning the LLM path — → 70.1% after PPO+GAE weight updates; prior SOTA 45.0% (+25.1 points).

AlphaEvolve TriMul CUDA-kernel task (H100; score = 1500/runtime): harness-only stalled at 0.120 (12,483 µs, 1.14×); entropic advantage weighting drove runtime to 1,017 µs — 14.02× speedup, score 1.475 vs 1.292 prior SOTA (12.4% faster), a 91.9% runtime cut from the harness-only peak.

MAGIC scRNA-seq denoising on pancreas data (mse norm, higher = better): harness-only hyperparameter sweeps (k, diffusion steps, bandwidth) plateaued at 0.241; the first GRPO checkpoint added a np.clip + np.rint rounding step → 0.289 vs 0.240 prior SOTA (+20.4%).
Ablation (Table 3): SIA-W+H strictly beats SIA-H everywhere, but the dominant lever flips by domain — harness updates did most of the LawBench work, weights nearly all of TriMul's (0.120 → 1.475).
advantages: Table 1's only system that edits harness and weights inside one self-improving loop; the nearest neighbours each stop short — Hyperagents co-evolves agent and improver but freezes weights, EUREKA composes scaffold-side reward generation with RL training but one-directionally.

RL algorithm choice is part of what the Feedback-Agent searches: PPO+GAE when per-step rewards are dense, GRPO when rollouts are cheap and the verifier fires at episode end, entropic advantage weighting when the reward histogram is right-skewed, plus REINFORCE+KL, best-of-N behavioral cloning (cold start), and DPO — selected per trajectory, not a fixed schedule.

Conditions on full per-instance trajectories (every prompt, tool call, extracted answer) rather than aggregate scores, so edits diagnose specific failure modes instead of mutating toward summary statistics.

Isolates each lever's contribution empirically: weight updates are shown to deliver knowledge no scaffold generation reached (the np.clip+np.rint invariant, H100 tiling patterns), directly answering RQ2 rather than asserting synergy.
limitations: Coupled co-evolutionary Goodhart (§8, the paper's own analysis): both levers optimise the same fixed verifier, so the harness finds scaffolds the current policy can exploit while the weights train on data from a scaffold that will change — the joint fixed point is a Nash equilibrium of two mutually blind optimisers, fragile off-distribution.
Lever and algorithm selection is a frozen LLM prior, not learned (§9); the loop alternates in coarse discrete rounds — finer interleaving is left as future work.

Three single-task evaluations, one base model (gpt-oss-120b), no seeds or variance reported; and §7.3's algorithm-selection guidance is 'common patterns observed' across tasks not reported here, with a fuller treatment deferred to v2.
2605.27276.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI at its merge point with test-time training: the capstone of the harness-school arc (DGM → Hyperagents → Continual Harness) that adds SEAL/TTRL-style weight updates as a second lever. Read after Continual Harness; pair with the sia repo card, whose --focus harness|weights flags split the loop the paper auto-selects.
2605.27276.reading: §3.2–3.3 (Feedback-Agent inputs, trajectory), §5.1–5.3 (lever selection), Table 3 and §6.3 per-task numbers, §7.3 (the six-algorithm menu and when each fires), §8 (coupled Goodhart).

2505.15734.tldr: No-label self-evolution: run RCR-prompted multi-agent debate, keep the consensus answer plus a consolidated rationale, GRPO-train the single model on them, then swap the evolved policy back into the debate team and repeat. +8.92 pts average on GSM-Plus after one round.
2505.15734.method: Agents A={a1..aN} debate a query for up to T rounds under the RCR prompt, which enforces three phases per round: Reflect (self-critique of own rationale), Critique (exactly two peers), Refine (update the answer, and any changed answer must add a novel reasoning step absent from all prior traces). Debate stops on unanimous consensus, else majority vote. Traces are compressed into one consolidated rationale R by keeping steps that recur across agents or introduce novel symbolic manipulation, yielding (q, y*, R). Training is GRPO on that instance with reward r = 2.0·1[y=y*] + 0.5·f_format(y) + 0.5·exp(−|y|/120) — the correctness term is agreement with the debate consensus, not ground truth. G=8 samples/query, clip 0.2, KL β=0.02, LoRA r=128 on attention/MLP projections, AdamW lr 5e-6. After each round the evolved policy replaces its own predecessor in the debate pool.
results: One DTE round (Table 1, GSM-Plus): Qwen-1.5B 42.00 → 55.92 (+13.92), Qwen-3B 61.75 → 69.50, Qwen-7B 68.62 → 74.71, Qwen-14B 71.79 → 78.88, Llama-3B 45.67 → 53.79, Llama-8B 55.62 → 66.17 — mean +8.92 pts over the base model at one forward pass. GSM8K gains average only +0.84 (models near ceiling) and ARC-Challenge is mixed: +3.67 Qwen-7B, +8.88 Llama-8B, but −0.85 Qwen-1.5B and −0.42 Qwen-3B. Across all five Table 1 benchmarks the evolved single model averages +3.06 pts over the base model and +1.09 pts over the 3-agent RCR committee that generated its traces.

Cross-domain transfer (Table 2): evolving on GSM8K gives +5.8 pts average on the unseen GSM-Plus, +2.5 on ARC-Challenge, and CommonsenseQA gains for 5/6 models; models ≥7B never lose more than 0.2 pts on any transfer task, while Qwen-1.5B drops 1.60 on ARC-Easy and 2.23 on CommonsenseQA. Evolving on GSM-Plus and testing on GSM8K is symmetric (+3.7 avg), which the authors read as learning heuristics (numeric decomposition, unit tracking) rather than dataset patterns.

The RCR prompt alone (ablation 1, eight models) beats the original MAD@3 prompt by +1.9 pts GSM8K, +3.7 GSM-Plus, +0.7 ARC-Challenge — up to +7.9 (Qwen-1.5B) and +6.1 (Qwen-7B) on GSM-Plus. It halves the mean sycophancy rate (0.28 → 0.13 on GSM-Plus) and narrows the verbosity gap by 43%, versus standard MAD where small-model sycophancy exceeds 28% on average.

GRPO beats both alternatives at fixed compute (Table 3, GSM-Plus, 10K steps): Qwen-1.5B 42.00 → SFT 47.31 / DPO 51.34 / GRPO 55.92; Qwen-3B 61.75 → SFT 58.33 (regression) / DPO 64.32 / GRPO 69.50; Qwen-7B 68.62 → 67.89 / 69.88 / 74.71. GRPO holds KL < 0.24 across sizes where DPO averages 0.43.

Effort scaling: 3 agents capture 85–95% of the achievable debate gain (ARC-Easy saturates at 2, GSM-Plus sometimes prefers 4–5; Qwen-7B peaks at 76.0% with 7 agents, +1.04 over 3). GRPO saturates near 8K steps (+0.32 pts average from 8K → 10K while wall-clock grows 25%). A second evolution round gives ≥7B at most +0.8 pts and often loses 0.4–1.4 (mean forgetting Fgt2 = 0.92 pts ≥7B, 1.6 smaller). Trace coverage is monotonic (Table 4): All-Traces beats Debate-Only by 4.43 pts and Random-2K by 9.17.
advantages: Self-referential where fixed-judge self-training is not: after each round the evolved policy replaces its own predecessor inside the debate ensemble (Algorithm 2, step 18), so trace generator and trace consumer improve together — and the evolved single model then beats the very committee (+1.09 pts on average across Table 1's five benchmarks) that produced its training data.

RCR is diagnosed before it is proposed: the paper first measures standard MAD's failure modes (sycophancy above 28% average for small models, verbosity bias, [correct → incorrect] transitions) and then fixes them mechanically — a fixed two-peer critique quota and a mandatory novel reasoning step on any answer change — halving sycophancy and cutting the verbosity gap 43%.

Design choices are ablated with a mechanism rather than asserted: GRPO over SFT/DPO at fixed compute with measured KL drift (< 0.24 vs 0.43), trace coverage shown monotonic across three sampling schemes, and temperature annealing justified by measured KL evolution (0.37 → 0.19 → 0.11 as T goes 1.0 → 0.4 → 0.0).

Operationally label-free: the reward's correctness term is exact-string agreement with the debate consensus, so no dataset labels and no external judge enter training; the generalization evidence (symmetric GSM8K↔GSM-Plus transfer, ≥7B losing ≤0.2 pts on any transfer task) is the paper's case that this is real reasoning gain, not overfitting.
limitations: Catastrophic forgetting under iteration, which the paper's own Limitations concedes it cannot eliminate ('potential model collapse' below 3B): at T=1.0, Round 2 loses 2.0 pts on GSM8K and gains only 13.5 pts on GSM-Plus, and Figure 2 shows Qwen-1.5B giving back 0.9 pts on GSM8K and 2.8 on GSM-Plus; Llama-3B at temperature 0.8 and 10K steps collapses to 2.73% on GSM8K and to 35.63 / 23.02 after two rounds. Temperature annealing 0.7 → 0.3 for ≤3B is a mitigation, not a fix — at T=0.4 Round-2 GSM-Plus is still 0.9 pts below Round 1.

The ceiling is the debate, not the data: the paper's Limitations says efficacy 'may degrade if debates are of poor quality or if initial agent performance is weak', and one round captures nearly all available gain — Round 2 adds at most +0.8 pts for ≥7B and more often loses 0.4–1.4 (mean forgetting Fgt2 0.92 pts ≥7B, 1.6 for smaller).

Scope is structured reasoning only (math, science MC-QA, commonsense); the paper flags open-ended generation and dialogue as unstudied, and states DTE still costs more to train than plain single-model fine-tuning.

Consensus errors propagate: correctness is agreement with the debate's majority answer, so a confident wrong consensus is a wrong training target — visible in Table 1 where Qwen-7B loses 2.35 pts on GSM8K and Qwen-7B / 1.5B lose on ARC-Challenge, with the paper attributing Round-1 Qwen-7B's GSM8K drop to traces that over-emphasised shortcut heuristics.
2505.15734.fits: Stage 6 Co-Evolution, the weight-persisting arm of debate: inference-time MAD (Du et al., Liang et al.) supplies the signal and GRPO writes it into the policy, replacing a per-query committee with one forward pass. Pairs with Agent0 and SOTOPIA-π as the three routes from a multi-agent signal to one trained model.
2505.15734.reading: §3.1 (measured MAD failure modes), §3.2 (RCR's three phases and the novel-step constraint), §3.3 (reward design, GRPO), §4.2 Tables 1–2, §4.3 ablations 1, 4, 5, 7 (RCR, GRPO vs SFT/DPO, trace selection, temperature).

2505.22954.tldr: The flagship empirical self-modifier: a coding agent edits its own source code, keeps only empirically-validated improvements, and archives them open-endedly.
results: Self-modification with archive-based evolution lets the agent improve the very code that runs its improvement loop.
Demonstrates compounding improvement over hand-crafted coding agents on coding tasks.
limitations: Validation is bounded by eval budget; self-edits can introduce bugs that must be caught by the evaluator.
2505.22954.fits: The 'does it actually work' answer to the Gödel Agent's 'what'. The Sakana blog is the best companion read. Run the repo (stage 10).
2505.22954.reading: Read the self-modification + validation loop (§3) and the archive (MAP-Elites-style) design (§4).

2504.15228.tldr: Minimal and transparent self-improvement: an agent with basic coding tools edits its own implementation, re-evaluates on benchmarks, and keeps only edits that help.
results: Gains from 17% to 53% on a random SWE-bench Verified subset, plus LiveCodeBench.
A data-efficient, non-gradient learning mechanism driven by reflection + code edits.
limitations: Evaluated on a random subset; gains can plateau as the agent exhausts easy self-edits.
2504.15228.fits: The simplest, most reproducible self-modifying agent — a great first read before DGM, which adds open-ended archives on top.
2504.15228.reading: Read the edit→evaluate→keep loop (§3) and the benchmark setup. Very short and concrete.

2408.06292.tldr: The first end-to-end ML research loop: generate ideas (novelty-checked), run experiments, plot and analyze, write a LaTeX paper, and score it with an automated reviewer — then iterate.
results: Produces complete papers at ~$15 each, with some results later independently reproduced/validated.
A fully reusable idea→paper→review loop for machine-learning research.
limitations: No vision experiments; occasionally mismatches idea and paper; the automated reviewer is weaker than human review; can hallucinate in the manuscript.
2408.06292.fits: The concrete 'AI doing AI research' baseline. v2 (stage 8) removes the template and adds agentic search; read both.
2408.06292.reading: Read the pipeline (§3) and the honest limitations (§6) — the limitations are as instructive as the method.

nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.tldr: Automates the entire research cycle — ideas, code, experiments, plots, manuscript, and peer review — end to end, in focused (template-scaffolded) and template-free open-ended (agentic tree search) modes.
results: Its generated manuscript passed first-round peer review at a top-tier ML workshop (70% acceptance rate).
Template-free agentic search expands exploration beyond human-provided scaffolds.
limitations: Still confined to machine-learning research; workshop peer review is not full top-conference review.
nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.fits: The peer-reviewed milestone that moves automated research from demo to capability. Compare its gains over v1 to see what 'removing the template' buys.
nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.reading: Read the two modes (§2–3) and the peer-review outcome; contrast with v1's limitations.

nature-funsearch-2024.tldr: A frozen LLM proposes candidate functions in a problem skeleton; a separate evaluator scores them; the best are fed back as few-shot examples — an evolutionary loop that found new mathematics.
results: Discovered new cap-set constructions (size 512 in dimension 8) — the first progress on the problem in years.
Also found an improved online bin-packing heuristic.
limitations: Needs a clean, fast evaluator; only works for problems expressible as program search.
nature-funsearch-2024.fits: The clearest proof that LLM + evaluator + evolution can produce *novel* results humans hadn't found. The model/evaluator split is the key lesson AlphaEvolve scales up.
nature-funsearch-2024.reading: Read the evaluate→select→prompt loop (§2–3) and the cap-set result. The DeepMind blog is a good companion.

2506.13131.tldr: A Gemini-powered coding agent that generates candidate algorithms, evaluates them (often with fast approximate evaluators over a distributed pool), and improves them via island-based evolutionary search.
results: Discovered a faster 4×4 matrix-multiplication algorithm (fewer multiplications than prior best) and improved kernels.
Improvements include components used to train AI systems — the stack improving the stack.
limitations: Depends on fast/approximate evaluators; specialized to algorithmic kernels rather than general code.
2506.13131.fits: FunSearch at industrial scale, aimed at *practical* algorithmic kernels. The most direct modern instance of 'AI improving the AI training stack'.
2506.13131.reading: Read the evaluator-guided evolution loop (§3) and the matrix-multiplication case; pair with the DeepMind blog.

1905.10985.tldr: Clune's agenda paper: instead of hand-designing intelligence piece by piece, treat the *learning algorithm itself* as the thing to be searched for.
1905.10985.method: Position paper: proposes three pillars for producing general AI — meta-learn the architecture, meta-learn the algorithm (evolve/search over learning algorithms), and meta-learn the environments — so the AI-generating algorithm (AI-GA) does the search, not humans.
results: Formalizes the 'AI-generating algorithm' thesis: learning is the search target, not the artifact.
Articulates the safety argument that AI-GAs avoid hand-designing intelligence and can be bounded by design.
limitations: Conceptual only — no working system; all three pillars remain open research programs.
1905.10985.fits: The philosophical blueprint for this entire list — nearly every later entry instantiates one of Clune's pillars (AutoML-Zero = pillar 2, POET = pillar 3).
1905.10985.reading: Read the three pillars (§2–4); it's short and defines the vocabulary the rest of the list uses.

frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.tldr: The survey that named 'Quality Diversity': optimize for a *collection* of diverse, high-performing solutions rather than a single optimum.
frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.method: Survey/position: QD algorithms return an archive of solutions indexed by a behavior/feature descriptor, seeking to illuminate the whole search space (diversity) while maximizing each niche's quality.
results: Defines the illumination objective — diversity + quality — as a distinct alternative to pure optimization.
Frames MAP-Elites, Novelty Search, and their hybrids as one family under a shared lens.
limitations: Survey, no new algorithm; the difficulty of choosing a meaningful behavior characterization is left open.
frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.fits: Why DGM and AlphaEvolve keep *archives* instead of one best answer — the QD objective is the substrate that lets self-improvement explore without collapsing.
frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.reading: Read the illumination framing (§2) and the MAP-Elites description; skim the taxonomy.

1504.04909.tldr: MAP-Elites: keep the best solution found in every cell of a behavior grid, illuminating the space of possible high-quality designs.
1504.04909.method: Map each individual to a low-dimensional behavior/feature descriptor; maintain a grid where each cell stores the best-performing solution for that niche (elitism); keep perturbing elites to fill and improve cells.
results: Illuminates search spaces (e.g., 6-legged robot gaits) where a single optimum hides useful alternatives.
Elite diversity provides robustness and reusable stepping stones for later search.
limitations: Needs a cheap, meaningful descriptor; scales poorly as descriptor dimensionality grows.
1504.04909.fits: The specific QD algorithm reused by DGM's archive — 'keep the best of every niche' is what lets open-ended self-improvement explore without collapse.
1504.04909.reading: Read the algorithm box (§3) and the gait experiments; the mechanism matters more than the domain.

1112.5309.tldr: POWERPLAY: continually invent the simplest problem you can't yet solve, learn it, and freeze the skill — growing a general solver from scratch.
1112.5309.method: Two coupled searches: one finds new tasks the current solver can't do (the 'simplest still unsolvable' problem), the other trains the solver to master them; each learned skill is added and frozen so later learning doesn't destroy it.
results: Demonstrates unsupervised task invention that grows capability without a predefined curriculum.
Frozen, reusable skills prevent catastrophic forgetting as new abilities accumulate.
limitations: Tiny hand-crafted domains; the 'simplest still unsolvable' criterion is hard to scale to real tasks.
1112.5309.fits: The earliest 'generate your own curriculum' loop — POET (stage 9) is its modern, evolutionary descendant.
1112.5309.reading: Read the two coupled search processes (§3); skim the experiments.

2309.03409.tldr: OPRO: use the LLM itself as the optimizer — feed it scored solution history and ask for better candidates, in natural language.
2309.03409.method: Prompt the LLM with the optimization problem plus a sorted history of (solution, score) pairs; it proposes new candidate solutions (prompts); evaluate them and repeat the loop.
results: Discovers novel, sometimes human-unreadable prompts (like 'Take a deep breath') that beat hand-designed prompts on GSM8K and Big-Bench Hard.
limitations: Optimization is meta-prompt/temperature sensitive; needs a reliable scalar score signal.
2309.03409.fits: The simplest 'LLM as optimizer' loop — the prompt becomes the search space. Ancestor of Promptbreeder and the whole optimization-as-language arc.
2309.03409.reading: Read the meta-prompt design (§3) and the discovered-prompts results (§5).

2309.16797.tldr: Promptbreeder: evolve a *population* of prompts — and evolve the mutation prompts too, making the self-improvement self-referential.
2309.16797.method: Maintain a population of task prompts plus 'mutation prompts' (thinking styles); an LLM mutates prompts, evaluates fitness on a training set, and the mutation-prompt level is itself evolved — a two-level self-improvement loop.
results: Evolved prompts outperform strong hand-crafted baselines on arithmetic, commonsense, and ethics benchmarks.
limitations: Expensive (many evaluations); fitness is domain-specific and can overfit the training set.
2309.16797.fits: The self-referential version of OPRO: it evolves not just prompts but the *mutator* of prompts.
2309.16797.reading: Read the population + self-referential mutation design (§3); skim results.

2310.04406.tldr: LATS: wrap a frozen LM in Monte Carlo Tree Search — the model acts, an LM value function scores, and reflection on failures backpropagates learning.
2310.04406.method: MCTS where the LM proposes actions, an LM-trained value function scores states, the environment returns rewards, and reflection on failed trajectories is injected back into search.
results: State-of-the-art at the time on HumanEval, HotpotQA, and WebShop among reasoning/agent frameworks.
limitations: High inference cost (tree search); needs an environment or reliable reward for the search to work.
2310.04406.fits: Shows a frozen model can be improved by the *scaffold* (search), not its weights — a core harness-RSI motif.
2310.04406.reading: Read the MCTS integration (§3) and how reflection feeds search (§4).

2303.17651.tldr: Self-Refine: the same model generates, critiques its own output, and refines — the minimal self-improvement loop.
2303.17651.method: Iterate: generate an output, have the *same* model critique it, refine based on that feedback, and repeat until a stop condition — no training, no extra data.
results: Improves across 7 tasks (dialogue, code, math, …) with no training or extra data, in just a few iterations.
limitations: Feedback quality is bounded by the model itself; can loop without converging (see 'Cannot Self-Correct').
2303.17651.fits: The minimal self-improvement loop — one model as both solver and critic. Most stage-3/4 work refines this.
2303.17651.reading: Read the feedback/refine loop (§2) and the ablation on feedback quality (§5).

2309.11495.tldr: Chain-of-Verification: draft, then plan *independent* verification questions, answer them in isolation, and produce a fact-checked final answer.
2309.11495.method: Four steps: draft a response; generate verification questions; answer each independently (to avoid bias from the draft); produce a final response conditioned on the verified facts.
results: Reduces hallucination on factoid QA (e.g., Wikidata) with no external tools or retraining.
limitations: Only covers facts the model can self-check; independent answers still draw from the same model.
2309.11495.fits: Verification-as-scaffold: decompose the check so the model can't just confirm its own error.
2309.11495.reading: Read the four-step pipeline (§3); note why 'independent answering' is the key design choice.

2305.11738.tldr: CRITIC: self-correction with *external tools* — search, an interpreter, and other tools gather corrective evidence before revising.
2305.11738.method: Generate → ask the model to critique its own output → use external tools (web search, code interpreter, etc.) to gather corrective evidence → revise against that grounded feedback.
results: Improves factuality (with search), code execution (with interpreter), and safety across several benchmarks.
limitations: Depends on tool availability/quality; still bounded by the model's revision ability.
2305.11738.fits: Adds *grounded* feedback to Self-Refine — the correction loop touches the real world instead of only self-assessing.
2305.11738.reading: Read the tool-interactive critique loop (§3) and one tool's results (§4).

2203.11171.tldr: Sampling many diverse chain-of-thought paths and taking a majority vote over their final answers lifts accuracy by roughly 3-24 points over greedy CoT, with no training, no verifier and no extra data.
2203.11171.method: Prompt the LM with the same few-shot chain-of-thought exemplars as Wei et al. (8 for arithmetic, 4-7 for commonsense), then replace greedy decoding with "sample-and-marginalize". Sample m reasoning paths (r_i, a_i) independently - T=0.5 with top-k=40 for UL2-20B and LaMDA-137B, T=0.7, k=40 for PaLM-540B, T=0.7 with no top-k for GPT-3 - and parse each final answer a_i after "The answer is". Marginalize out the latent paths by majority vote, argmax_a sum_i 1(a_i=a); main results average 10 runs of 40 paths. No training, verifier, re-ranker or annotation - a "self-ensemble" over a single model. Aggregation was ablated: unweighted majority vote (74.4 GSM8K) matches length-normalized probability weighting (74.1), because normalized path probabilities are too close to discriminate; unnormalized weighting collapses to 59.9.
results: GPT-3 code-davinci-002: GSM8K 60.1 -> 78.0 (+17.9), SVAMP 75.8 -> 86.8 (+11.0), AQuA 39.8 -> 52.0 (+12.2), MultiArith 96.2 -> 100.0, CSQA 79.0 -> 81.5 - new SoTA without any supervised fine-tuning.
Gains scale with model size: UL2-20B only +3.2 to +6.8 points (GSM8K 4.1 -> 7.3) vs LaMDA-137B +9.1 to +23.9 (MultiArith 51.8 -> 75.7, GSM8K 17.1 -> 27.7), and GPT-3 code-davinci-001 +6.7 to +23.2.

Beats other uses of the same compute at matched budget: vs beam search on UL2-20B AQuA (beam-40 = 10.2, beam-1 = 23.6 vs self-consistency 26.9 +/- 0.5 over 40 sampled paths); vs prompt ensembles on LaMDA-137B GSM8K (3 prompt sets 18.6, 40 prompt permutations 19.2 vs 27.7); vs multi-model ensembles (LaMDA-137B + PaLM-540B = 36.9 vs 74.4 for PaLM-540B alone).

Robust and re-usable elsewhere: holds across three prompt sets (PaLM GSM8K 74.4 / 72.1 / 70.4), across sampling parameters (T, top-k, nucleus p), on imperfect CoT prompts (LaMDA-137B GSM8K 14.9 -> 23.4, above the 17.1 of a correct prompt with greedy decode), equation-only rationales, and zero-shot CoT (PaLM 43.0 -> 69.2).
advantages: Establishes inference-time diversity plus answer agreement as a training-free accuracy lever: new SoTA on GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA and StrategyQA with no additional training, annotation or auxiliary model - beating prior work that required fine-tuning on 7.5k examples plus a second 175B verifier (GSM8K 55 vs 74.4).

Shows the gain comes from diversity of reasoning paths, not merely from more samples: it dominates beam search (which degrades as beams grow, 23.6 -> 10.2 AQuA), sample-and-rank, prompt-order and multi-prompt ensembles, and cross-model ensembles, at equal sample count.

Turns agreement into a usable uncertainty signal: the share of decodes agreeing with the majority answer correlates strongly with accuracy, giving a calibration / "know when it doesn't know" estimate for free.

The primitive is portable and cheap: compatible with any sampling scheme, with zero-shot CoT and with non-natural-language rationales (equations); majority-vote-over-self-samples is the mechanism later RSI pipelines inherit for aggregating debate (stage 6) and for filtering self-generated data.
limitations: Cost multiplies with the number of paths (40 in the main results) for one final answer; the paper's own advice is to start with 5-10 paths, since the accuracy curve saturates quickly.
It only applies where the final answer comes from a fixed answer set that can be parsed and counted; open-ended generation needs an externally defined consistency metric.

The model cannot distinguish good reasoning from bad: normalized path probabilities cluster closely enough that probability weighting adds nothing over vote counting, and the paper notes models still emit incorrect or nonsensical rationales (the StrategyQA population figures in Table 4), leaving rationale grounding to future work.

No correctness guarantee - agreement is only a proxy, and the premise that correct reasoning is more consistent than incorrect reasoning is argued by intuition rather than proved, so a confidently wrong majority survives the vote.
2203.11171.fits: Stage 3's founding inference-time result and the baseline the stage's papers argue against: nothing is revised, reliability comes from aggregating diverse samples of one frozen model. Debate aggregation (stage 6) and consistency filtering of self-generated data inherit the primitive. Pairs with Self-Refine; the negative result targets revision, not voting.
2203.11171.reading: §2 (sample-and-marginalize and why majority vote matches probability weighting - Table 1) and §3.2 Table 2 for the headline numbers; §3.4 Tables 6-7 for the beam-search and ensemble baselines. Skim §4 and the appendix figures.

2305.20050.tldr: Let's Verify Step by Step: reward *each reasoning step* (process supervision), not just the final answer — and show it beats outcome supervision.
2305.20050.method: Train a reward model with process supervision — feedback on every intermediate step, not just the final result — and use it to rank/generate solutions; active learning picks which steps to label.
results: Process-supervised RM solves 78.2% of MATH vs. 72.4% for outcome supervision; step-level active learning is notably data-efficient.
limitations: Requires expensive step-level human labels; the PRM is itself a large trained model.
2305.20050.fits: Shows *where* feedback is placed changes what a self-improving system learns — the verification layer is itself trainable.
2305.20050.reading: Read the process vs. outcome supervision contrast (§2–3) and the MATH result.

2310.01798.tldr: The counterweight: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without external feedback. Intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy on GSM8K, CommonSenseQA and HotpotQA across GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2, and multi-agent debate loses to self-consistency at equal inference cost.
2310.01798.method: A measurement protocol, not a method. Each trial uses a three-step prompt: (1) initial generation, (2) review that answer and emit feedback, (3) re-answer the question conditioned on the feedback — capped at two correction rounds. Two conditions are contrasted: oracle-guided, where a ground-truth stop check prevents the model from altering an already-correct answer, and intrinsic, where the model alone decides whether to revise. Benchmarks: GSM8K (1,319 problems), CommonSenseQA dev (1,221), HotpotQA closed-book exact match (100). Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 and GPT-4 (temperature 1), GPT-4-Turbo-1106 and Llama-2-70b-chat (temperature 0). Two follow-up controls: replicating multi-agent debate (3 agents, 2 rounds, gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Du et al.'s own prompts) against self-consistency at matched response counts, and re-running Self-Refine's constrained-generation setup with the task constraint moved into the initial prompt.
results: Oracle labels are what made prior work look good (Table 2): GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0; GPT-4 95.5 -> 97.5, 82.0 -> 85.5, 49.0 -> 59.0.

Intrinsic self-correction degrades every model (Tables 3-4). GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0 and 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0 and 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo: 91.5 -> 88.0 -> 90.0 (GSM8K), 84.0 -> 81.5 -> 83.0 (CSQA). Llama-2-70b-chat collapses: 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5 and 64.0 -> 37.5 -> 36.5. Three alternative feedback prompts do not rescue it (Tables 5-6): every variant still ends below its single-call baseline (GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 -> 88.0/90.0/91.0; Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 -> down to 30.5-58.0).

Multi-agent debate is self-consistency in disguise (Table 7, GSM8K): standard prompting 76.7 (1 response); debate 82.5 at 3 responses vs self-consistency 83.2; debate 83.0 at 9 responses vs self-consistency 88.2 — debate loses outright once response counts are matched.

The Self-Refine gain was a bad initial prompt (Table 8, CommonGen-Hard concept coverage): Madaan et al. standard 44.0 -> 67.0 with 7 calls, but adding 'includes *ALL* of the above concepts' to the initial prompt gives 81.8 with 1 call — and self-correction on top of that drops it to 75.1.

Why it degrades (Section 3.3, Figure 1): GPT-3.5 keeps its GSM8K answer unchanged 74.7% of the time, and among the rest, correct -> incorrect flips outnumber incorrect -> correct fixes; GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo retain their initial answers more often than the weaker models.
advantages: Isolates the label leak that inflated the whole self-correction literature: it reproduces RCI's and Reflexion's reported gains, then shows they vanish the moment the oracle correctness label used as a stopping criterion is removed (Table 1 gives the per-paper taxonomy).

Establishes the equal-inference-cost baseline as a norm — self-consistency at the same number of responses — and shows multi-agent debate only matches it at 3 responses and falls 5.2 points behind at 9, so the improvement is selection, not correction.

Falsifies the Self-Refine improvement by construction rather than argument: folding the feedback prompt's missing constraint into the initial prompt beats 7 self-correction calls using 1 call, identifying prompt asymmetry as the source of the claimed gain.
The negative result is not a sampling artifact of one model or decoding scheme: it replicates across four models, two temperatures (0 and 1), three benchmarks, and four different feedback prompts.
limitations: The paper's own Section 7 scope limit: this evaluates reasoning only, and the authors expect self-correction to remain useful where the model can actually assess the response, e.g. preference, style or safety alignment — the failure is specific to judging reasoning correctness.

Coverage is a fixed menu: four 2023-2024 models, at most two correction rounds, one three-step prompt template family, and 200 sampled questions per dataset for every model except GPT-3.5 (HotpotQA only 100, a size the authors themselves call too small for the Section 3.3 answer-change statistics, footnote 1). No variance or significance is reported anywhere.

The Section 4 debate replication is a re-implementation: same prompts but gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 on the full 1,319-question test set instead of the original's 100 examples, so the head-to-head is not bit-identical to Du et al.
Aim is measurement, not repair: it names external feedback (code executors, search, trained verifiers, humans) as the escape route but proposes and evaluates no new self-correction method of its own.
2310.01798.fits: Stage-3 negative control — the measurement discipline every self-correction claim in this catalog has to survive. Pairs directly with Reflexion and RCI (whose gains it traces to oracle labels), Self-Refine (its prompt-design critique), Du et al. multi-agent debate (the equal-cost baseline), and stage-4 verifier work, which is the external-feedback escape route it recommends.
2310.01798.reading: Read Section 3 (Tables 2-4 plus Figure 1's answer-change analysis), Section 4 (Table 7, debate vs self-consistency), Section 5 (Table 8, prompt design), and Section 7. Appendix A has the verbatim prompts.

2308.10144.tldr: ExpeL: distill successful trajectories into an insight rule-base, reflect on failures to revise it, and retrieve insights at inference — no weight updates.
2308.10144.method: Two phases: (1) gather successful trajectories and extract natural-language insights; (2) on failure, reflect and update the insight base — then retrieve relevant insights to guide future attempts.
results: Consistent gains on HotpotQA and ALFWorld vs. strong baselines (e.g., Reflexion), including transfer of insights across similar tasks.
limitations: Extraction/retrieval quality is the bottleneck; open-ended but bounded by the insight bank.
2308.10144.fits: The 'distill trajectories into a rule base' memory agent — bridges Reflexion's episodic memory toward persistent, transferable principles.
2308.10144.reading: Read the insight extraction + success/failure split (§3); note the transfer experiment.

2502.12110.tldr: A-MEM: memory as a Zettelkasten-style linked graph that *reorganizes itself* — an agentic memory system, not a fixed store.
2502.12110.method: Structures memories as linked notes with context and timestamps; a memory agent dynamically creates, links, and updates memories from new dialogs, so organization evolves with experience.
results: Improves recall and downstream QA on LoCoMo and other long-context memory benchmarks over fixed-structure memory.
limitations: Graph organization depends on the memory agent's decisions; retrieval can still surface irrelevant nodes.
2502.12110.fits: Memory that reorganizes itself — the memory system is an agent. Sets up the 'evolve the memory' line (MemEvolve).
2502.12110.reading: Read the memory formation + evolution loops (§3–4) and the LoCoMo results.

2305.10250.tldr: MemoryBank adds persistent long-term memory to frozen LLMs: timestamped dialogue logs with LLM-written event summaries and user portraits, FAISS dense retrieval, and an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve that decays unreinforced memories — demonstrated in SiliconFriend, an empathetic companion chatbot.
2305.10250.method: Storage has three tiers: timestamped multi-turn dialogue logs; LLM-generated daily event summaries rolled up into a global summary; and daily personality insights aggregated into a global user portrait (fixed prompts, e.g. "Summarize the events and key information in the content [dialog/events]"). Each dialogue turn and summary is a memory piece, embedded (MiniLM for English, Text2vec for Chinese) and indexed in FAISS via LangChain, DPR-style dual-tower retrieval. At interaction time the current conversation is the query; retrieved memories plus the global portrait and event summary are packed into the prompt. Updating applies the Ebbinghaus curve R = e^(−t/S): retention R decays with elapsed time t; strength S starts at 1 on first mention, and each recall increments S by 1 and resets t to 0, so re-accessed memories persist longer. Open-source variants add LoRA tuning (rank 16, 3 epochs, one A100) on 38k psychological dialogues.
results: Quantitative eval: 194 hand-written probing questions (97 English, 97 Chinese) over a simulated 10-day memory store of 15 ChatGPT-role-played users; human annotators scored retrieval accuracy, response correctness, coherence, and ranking (s = 1/rank).
SiliconFriend_ChatGPT is best overall: English retrieval 0.763, correctness 0.716, coherence 0.912, ranking 0.818 (Chinese: 0.711 / 0.655 / 0.675 / 0.758).

Open-source variants match or beat retrieval (BELLE 0.814 EN / 0.856 ZH; ChatGLM 0.809 / 0.84) but lag sharply on correctness (0.418–0.603) and coherence — attributed to weaker base models, not the memory layer.

Qualitatively, an online SiliconFriend platform collected real user conversations; the paper shows it recalling a recommended book and a quicksort request days later and correctly denying an undiscussed heap-sort session.
The forgetting curve itself is never quantified: no ablation or number isolates its effect, and the paper flags the model as exploratory.
advantages: Early (May 2023) mechanism giving both closed-source (ChatGPT) and open-source (ChatGLM 6.2B, BELLE 7B) LLMs persistent, evolving memory with no weight changes — the memory layer alone, plus optional LoRA for empathy tuning.
Forgetting-as-feature: time-decayed retention with reinforcement on recall (spacing effect) replaces append-only logs or fixed-window truncation with an anthropomorphic update policy.
Memory is more than retrieval: hierarchical daily-to-global summaries plus a user portrait let the bot adapt to personality, not just look up facts.
Practical and bilingual: swappable embedders and backbones, released as working SiliconFriend code.
limitations: The paper itself calls the Ebbinghaus update "exploratory and highly simplified": S is a bare integer counter, and no experiment measures whether forgetting helps or hurts.
Quantitative evaluation is fully simulated — ChatGPT role-plays all 15 users and generates the dialog history — with only 194 probing questions scored by annotators.
Summary-based storage discards detail: correctness for open-source backbones falls to 0.42–0.60, so specific recall is unreliable even when retrieval succeeds.
Scoped to companion/counseling interactions of 10 simulated days; far shorter than real long-horizon deployment.
2305.10250.fits: Stage 4's "memory as database with decay" baseline: an external store passively written, densely retrieved, and decayed by a hand-set curve — the update policy is fixed by design, never learned. A-MEM makes memory agentic (LLM organizes and links notes into a graph); MemEvolve evolves the memory system's own architecture.
2305.10250.reading: §2 covers the three components (storage 2.1, FAISS retrieval 2.2, Ebbinghaus update 2.3 — the R = e^(−t/S) rules); §3.1 for the 38k-dialogue LoRA tuning; Table 2 for all numbers. §4.1 examples are skippable.

2604.15097.tldr: Strategy Genes: skill *documents* are unstable control; compact 'strategy genes' (skill IDs + parameters) control and evolve more reliably.
2604.15097.method: 4.6k controlled trials across 45 code scenarios: compare documentation-oriented skill packages vs. compact 'strategy genes' (skill identifiers + config); show compact, stable representations control and evolve better.
results: Expanding compact experience into fuller docs often fails to help and can degrade average performance.
Compact strategy genes give stabler test-time control and a cleaner substrate for iterative evolution.
limitations: Beta technical report; results are specific to code-solving scenarios.
2604.15097.fits: A warning for the skill-library paradigm (Voyager/ACE): bigger skill docs ≠ better control. The 'gene' framing links memory evolution to evolutionary RSI.
2604.15097.reading: Read the skill-package vs. strategy-gene comparison (§3) and the controlled-trial design.

2602.07755.tldr: ALMA meta-learns the memory design itself: a GPT-5 Meta Agent searches memory designs written as executable Python, reflecting on archived designs and their eval logs, and the discovered designs beat Trajectory Retrieval, ReasoningBank, Dynamic Cheatsheet and G-Memory on all four sequential-decision benchmarks.
2602.07755.method: The Meta Agent (GPT-5) runs open-ended exploration over memory designs expressed as executable Python — code is the search space, so Turing completeness theoretically admits any design. Designs implement two abstract classes: MemoStructure with general_update/general_retrieve orchestrating sub-module layers, and Sub_memo_layer with its own update/retrieve and optional database; layers chain, so one sub-module's output feeds the next. Each step samples up to 5 archived designs without replacement (probability set by success rate and inverse visit count, tau=0.5, alpha=0.5 visit penalty, all probabilities non-zero), reflects on the sampled design's source, success rate and interaction logs to plan, implements a new design in code, trial-runs it (up to 3 debugger reflections on runtime errors), then evaluates and archives it with metrics and logs. 11 steps discover 43 designs. Evaluation is two-phase: memory is collected from memory-free trajectories, then deployment success rate is measured (static mode during learning, dynamic mode for distribution shift).
results: GPT-5-nano agentic system, four benchmarks: overall success 6.1% (no memory) to 12.3% (+6.2) for the best-learned design, above every human baseline (G-Memory 7.7, Trajectory Retrieval 8.6, ReasoningBank 7.5, Dynamic Cheatsheet 7.2); ALFWorld 2.9% to 12.4% (+9.5), Baba Is AI 9.5% to 19.0% (+9.5).

Transferred unchanged to a stronger GPT-5-mini agentic system: overall 41.1% (no memory) to 53.9% (+12.8), again above all human baselines; ALFWorld 67.6% to 87.1% (+19.5). The 12.8 vs 6.2 delta of 6.6% exceeds that of every human-designed memory, i.e. learned designs help stronger models more.

Ablation, greedy search on ALFWorld at the same 43-design budget: best-learned 11.9% (GPT-5-nano) and 77.1% (GPT-5-mini) versus 12.4% and 87.1% from open-ended exploration — the archive's stepping-stone sampling is what buys the gain.

Task distribution shift (memory collected from 70 valid-seen ALFWorld tasks, deployed in dynamic mode on valid unseen, GPT-5-mini): learned design 84.1%, outperforming all human baselines; Fig. 4 shows it also reaches higher success sooner as collection task count grows (better sample efficiency).

Cost (Fig. 6): 53.9% average success at $0.09 end-to-end memory cost, lower than all handcrafted baselines, with 1,319 retrieved tokens per task versus 9,149 (Trajectory Retrieval), 6,095 (G-Memory) and 2,258 (Dynamic Cheatsheet).
advantages: The searched object is the memory architecture itself — which databases exist (embedding, graph, dictionary), what is stored, how it is retrieved and updated — as one evolvable Python file, so it sits a meta-level above this catalog's fixed memory designs (ACE playbooks, G-Memory, Dynamic Cheatsheet) rather than tuning them.

It specializes per domain instead of reusing one recipe: Fig. 3 shows learned ALFWorld/TextWorld designs built on spatial relations, affordance graphs and trajectory schemas, while Baba Is AI and MiniHack designs converge on abstract strategy libraries and plan synthesis.

Open-ended archive search is shown to beat greedy selection at equal exploration budget (Appendix C.2, Fig. 14), and the resulting code plus logs are the artifact — the learned design transfers across evaluator FMs without retuning.

Efficiency falls out without being optimized for: no cost term in the objective, yet the best-learned design is cheaper per memory than every handcrafted baseline, which the authors read as an argument for adding multi-objective Pareto search as future work.
limitations: Memory designs are learned offline against a fixed learning set; the authors deliberately skip online learning of designs because evaluating each candidate needs many rollouts and would blow the compute budget — an adaptive continual learner should discover designs from dynamic data.

Scope is token-level memory only: parametric and latent memory are explicitly out of scope, chosen because explicit token memory evaluates faster without extra model training and is more interpretable and transferable.

Model-generated memory code executes inside the agentic loop, so designs are run in isolated sandboxes and human-inspected for harmful behavior such as prompt injection; the paper calls for systematic inspection as the system scales.

Evidence is four text-based sequential decision-making benchmarks (ALFWorld, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack) with one fixed agentic system per run; each domain needs its own 11-step, 43-design search.
2602.07755.fits: Stage 4 (Harness-level RSI), Context & Memory Evolution: the memory-design-as-search-space counterpart to ACE's context playbooks and MemEvolve's meta-evolution of memory systems — ALMA's related work names MemEvolve as the concurrent work, contrasting open-ended archive search with MemEvolve's handcrafted initializations plus greedy selection. It replaces the fixed memory loops of Reflexion and ExpeL.
2602.07755.reading: §3.1–3.3 (code search space, two-phase evaluation, archive sampling); §4.1–4.4 with Table 1 for the numbers; Appendix A.1 for the MemoStructure/Sub_memo_layer classes, A.6 pseudocode, C.2 greedy ablation, Fig. 6 cost.

2607.14159.tldr: MemoHarness: optimize the whole agent *harness* (context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding) — and learn it from the agent's own executions.
2607.14159.method: Frames the harness as the optimization target; MemoHarness learns harness policies from its own execution traces rather than optimizing a single narrow artifact like a prompt.
results: Adaptive per-case harnesses improve agent behavior vs. a single global harness.
limitations: Large harness search space; needs execution feedback to attribute harness edits to outcomes.
2607.14159.fits: Expands the self-improvement target from prompts/pipelines to the *whole harness* — the bridge from stage-4 memory to stage-5 harness evolution.
2607.14159.reading: Read how harness components are parameterized and learned (§3–4).

2607.26784.tldr: SkillRise: learn reusable skills *across* related tasks with a unified RL objective and progressive curricula — not per-task retries.
2607.26784.method: Unified RL framework that groups related task instances into progressive curricula and learns transferable skills across tasks, replacing per-task RL and multi-stage extraction/retrieval/execution pipelines.
results: Cross-task skill learning outperforms per-task RL and pipeline-based skill baselines.
limitations: Requires tasks that genuinely share solution patterns; RL sample cost.
2607.26784.fits: Unifies skill acquisition with RL so skills transfer — closing the gap between Voyager-style skill libraries and agentic RL.
2607.26784.reading: Read the curriculum grouping + unified RL objective (§3–4).

2512.18746.tldr: MemEvolve: evolve the memory *system itself* — its storage, distillation, and tool synthesis — not just its contents.
2512.18746.method: Treat the memory architecture (storage, distillation, tool synthesis) as the evolving object: an outer evolutionary loop mutates and selects memory-system designs, removing the 'static memory' bottleneck.
results: Evolving the memory system yields gains over manually engineered memory across agent tasks.
limitations: Evolutionary search over memory architectures is expensive; gains are environment-dependent.
2512.18746.fits: The 'evolve the memory, not just use it' position — one level above agent-level evolution. Pairs with ALMA as two routes to the same target.
2512.18746.reading: Read how the memory-system space is encoded and evolved (§3–4).

2607.05297.tldr: MetaSkill-Evolve: recursive skill improvement — a fast loop rewrites task skills, a slow loop evolves the meta-skill that improves skills.
2607.05297.method: Two-timescale loop: a fast loop rewrites task skills from execution traces; a slow loop evolves the meta-skill (the skill that improves skills), making self-improvement recursive rather than one-level.
results: Recursive improvement of the skill-improver yields gains beyond non-recursive skill rewriting.
limitations: Two-timescale stability is tricky; recursive gain can plateau.
2607.05297.fits: Makes skill evolution actually *recursive* — the improver is itself improved, the definitional move of RSI applied to skills.
2607.05297.reading: Read the two-timescale separation (§3) and how the meta-skill is updated.

2604.25850.tldr: Agentic Harness Engineering: automate harness evolution by instrumenting three things — components, trajectories, and edit attribution.
2604.25850.method: Closed loop over three observability pillars: (1) component observability (track each harness component), (2) trajectory observability (surface actionable signal in long traces), (3) attribution (link edits to effects) — to automate harness editing for coding agents.
results: Automatic harness evolution improves coding-agent performance where manual harness tuning was the bottleneck.
limitations: Observability infrastructure is heavy; attribution of edits remains approximate.
2604.25850.fits: Turns harness engineering from manual craft into a measurable, closed-loop process — the instrumentation prerequisite for all stage-5 harness evolution.
2604.25850.reading: Read the three observability pillars (§3) and the attribution mechanism (§4).

2608.12307.tldr: AI4AI at Test-Time: a strong builder model constructs inference-time harnesses that help a *weaker* model — strong-to-weak transfer with no weight updates.
2608.12307.method: A strong builder model constructs inference-time harnesses/scaffolds that let a weaker target model solve tasks more reliably — strong-to-weak distillation, but at test time with no parameter updates.
results: Builder-constructed harnesses improve weak-model reliability across four representative Theory-of-Mind benchmarks.
limitations: Transfer is bounded by what the harness can express; no durable gain (the weak model is unchanged).
2608.12307.fits: Harness as a *transfer* channel: the improving intelligence lives in the scaffold, not the weights — a clean contrast to SIA's joint weight updates.
2608.12307.reading: Read the strong-to-weak scaffolding setup (§3) and the four-benchmark results.

2603.03329.tldr: AutoHarness: automatically synthesize a code harness of guards so the agent can't take illegal actions (like the illegal chess moves behind 78% of Gemini losses).
2603.03329.method: The LLM synthesizes a code harness around the agent — a guard layer that wraps raw actions so illegal ones are caught or blocked before execution.
results: Auto-synthesized harnesses eliminate illegal-move failures and improve agent reliability.
limitations: Covers only actions anticipated at synthesis time; needs re-synthesis as the domain shifts.
2603.03329.fits: The 'safety-rail as harness' perspective — self-improvement by constraining the action space, complementing the exploration-focused harness work.
2603.03329.reading: Read the harness-synthesis loop (§3) and the chess case study.

2608.05446.tldr: EvoHarness-RL makes harness use a learned policy: a BPE workspace (Belief/Progress/Experience) with four meta-actions (track/commit/recall/note) is taught by SFT then cost-aware GRPO, lifting Qwen3-8B on ALFWorld from 47.9% to 96.9% seen, 86.6% unseen.
2608.05446.method: EvoHarness-RL externalizes the workspace into BPE state Ht=(Bt,Pt,Et): Belief (ALFWorld: a rule-based world-state tracker updated after each environment step), Progress (a bounded committed-subgoal list), Experience (a four-category skill bank — general, task-specific, common mistakes, object→location search priors — with keyword-overlap recall, LFU eviction, 80 entries/category). The policy interleaves four meta-actions with environment actions under one shared step budget: track [object|world], commit [subgoal], recall [query], note [insight]. Stage 1, supervised harness fine-tuning: SFT Qwen3-8B on 87 successful Claude-Opus teacher trajectories (1,153 next-action pairs from 500 games; teacher makes 405 harness calls, ~18% of turns), whose accumulated store seeds the skill bank. Stage 2, cost-aware GRPO from that checkpoint: R = 10·1[solved] + success-gated efficiency term max(0,1−|τ|/70) + cosine-annealed action-diversity bonus − spam/invalid-format penalties, KL β=0.01 to the SFT reference. At epoch boundaries an external consolidation model merges buffered notes into the bank via add/update/remove.
results: ALFWorld seen split, Qwen3-8B (140-task validation): ReAct 47.9% → prompt-time BPE 56.4% → SFT 68.6% → GRPO 96.9% (+49.0 over ReAct); beats trainable baselines GRPO 65.6%, SkillOS 80.2%, SkillRL 89.9%, and matches Claude Opus 4.5 ReAct (96.4%; 98.5% with the prompt-time BPE harness)
Unseen split: 50.0% (ReAct) → 77.6% (prompt-time BPE) → 69.4% (SFT, a drop) → 86.6% (RL) — cost-aware GRPO recalibrates harness access that imitation over-fits to seen tasks
Prompt-time BPE alone lifts frontier models: GPT-4.1 47.9 → 70.0 (+22.1), GPT-5 60.7 → 85.0 (+25.7), Claude Opus 4.5 96.4 → 98.5
Component ablation (frozen Qwen3-8B, prompt-time BPE): removing any of Belief/Progress/Experience drops 56.4% into the 48.6–50.7% range, with Experience removal the lowest (48.6%, §3.3)

Two dynamics: harness annealing — mean harness calls fall from the SFT scaffold's frequent use to ≈1 per episode, recall persisting while commit/note decay to ~0 (Figs. 3, 5); harness evolution — add/update/remove consolidation plus LFU eviction keep the skill bank compact while training reward stays above standard GRPO throughout (Fig. 6)
advantages: Makes harness access a first-class learnable decision: harness actions spend the same step budget as environment actions, so the policy learns when external state is worth its cost — the mechanism behind both the SFT→RL seen jump (68.6→96.9) and the unseen recovery (69.4→86.6, where SFT alone underperforms the 77.6 prompt-time harness)

Unifies within-episode state tracking (Belief, Progress) and cross-episode skill curation (Experience) under one policy-facing interface and one four-action protocol; the paper's position is that prior self-evolving agents keep these two separated

Names and evidences two co-evolutionary dynamics — harness annealing (the policy internalizes routine scaffold calls, with action-specific decay rates in Fig. 5) and harness evolution (consolidation plus LFU eviction yield a compact, revisable skill bank rather than append-only memory) — while Fig. 6 rules out policy collapse as the explanation for fewer calls

Cheap, inspectable grounding: the ALFWorld harness is deterministic where possible (rule-based belief parser, keyword-overlap recall, LFU eviction); no LLM calls sit inside the rollout loop, and consolidation runs outside it at epoch boundaries
limitations: Single-environment evidence: everything is ALFWorld, and Appendix A concedes the learned action mix is environment-dependent — it 'should not be interpreted as learning a fixed universal harness-action distribution'; Belief/Progress/Experience emphasis would shift in SWE or visually grounded settings

SFT alone generalizes worse than the prompt-time harness (69.4% vs 77.6% unseen): supervised imitation copies teacher harness-use patterns without learning when access is worthwhile; only GRPO fixes it

Dense reward shaping is load-bearing: with success as a sparse 10·1[solved] gate, the time-annealed diversity bonus, spam/format penalties, and cosine curriculum are all needed to keep the policy from ignoring harness actions or falling into repetition loops

Frontier-model dependence in the loop's periphery: Claude Opus supplies all 87 SFT trajectories (kept from 500 games) and every consolidation add/update/remove decision; the belief tracker is also only a rule-based parser, adequate for ALFWorld's text state
2608.05446.fits: Stage 5 (Harness-level RSI), the RL flavor: rather than searching or rewriting scaffold code (AutoHarness, SoL-Pi, Continual Harness) or distilling a harness into weights (Harness-Zero), it keeps the harness implementation fixed and trains the policy to construct and access its state while the experience store co-evolves. Pairs with ACE (evolving context) and the SkillOS/SkillRL baselines it beats.
2608.05446.reading: §2 end-to-end (BPE, action protocol, Eqs. 1–6); §3.2–3.4 with Tables 1–3 for numbers; §4 + Appendix A for annealing/evolution dynamics; Appendix B case study; Appendix C for implementation and Table 4 hyperparameters.

2603.19461.tldr: Hyperagents merge the task agent and the agent that improves it into one editable program, so the improvement mechanism itself evolves — metacognitive self-modification — removing the DGM's fixed handcrafted instruction-generation layer and its coding-only task/self-modification alignment assumption.
2603.19461.method: A hyperagent is one editable Python program containing a task agent (solves the task; initially a single FM call) and a meta agent, whose only job is to modify any part of the codebase given the repo path, past evaluation results, and remaining iterations.
