DGM-H wraps this in DGM's open-ended loop: sample a parent from the archive (probability proportional to performance, inversely proportional to successfully compiled children — score-child-prop), let it metacognitively self-modify, stage-eval the child (small task subset first; zero on any failed domain), and add survivors to the archive. Because the instruction-generation mechanism, memory, and tooling are all code inside the search space, the meta agent rewrites how future improvements are generated (e.g., performance tracking, persistent memory). Only the outer loop — parent selection and evaluation protocol — stays handcrafted in the main experiments; Appendix E.5 relaxes parent selection.
results: Polyglot (80 iterations, DGM's exact setup, 5 runs): training 50-task subset 0.140 → 0.340 (CI 0.300–0.380), full benchmark 0.084 → 0.267 (CI 0.231–0.280) — comparable to DGM's 0.380/0.307 despite not being handcrafted for coding

Beyond coding (100 iterations, joint paper-review + robotics runs): paper-review test 0.0 → 0.710 (CI 0.590–0.750), beating the AI-Scientist-v2 reviewer baseline (0.630); robotics reward design 0.060 → 0.372 (CI 0.355–0.436) vs the directly-optimizing default reward (0.348), discovering jumping gaits over the standing-tall local optimum

Baselines (test, both domains): unmodified DGM 0.0/0.0; manually customized DGM-custom 0.590/0.348 (still p<0.05 below DGM-H); DGM-H w/o self-improve — a fixed meta agent, i.e. ADAS — 0.0/0.213; w/o open-ended exploration 0.0/0.116; all significantly worse (Wilcoxon p<0.05)

Transfer, measured by imp@50 on held-out IMO-level math grading: hyperagents transferred from paper-review/robotics runs reach 0.630 (CI 0.540–0.630), vs imp@50 = 0.0 for the initial meta agent (both DGM and DGM-H variants) and 0.0 (CI 0.0–0.010) for DGM-custom transfer agents — the meta improvements (performance tracker, persistent memory) are general, not domain-specific

Compounding and the outer loop: 200 iterations from transfer hyperagents score 0.640 vs 0.610 from scratch (n.s., higher median); initialized from ProofAutoGrader it lifts full IMO-GradingBench accuracy 0.561 → 0.601 (MAE 0.178 → 0.175); Appendix E.5's evolved parent selection (rediscovered UCB, adaptive-temperature softmax) reaches 0.491 vs 0.428 random, still below handcrafted score-child-prop 0.532
advantages: First demonstration that the improvement mechanism itself can be left to evolve, with the gains shown transferable (imp@50 0.630 vs 0.0 for DGM-custom transfers) and attributable to named acquired machinery — a PerformanceTracker over performance_history.json and a persistent memory of insights/hypotheses/plans shown as real evolved code and memory entries (Appendix E.3)

Drops DGM's load-bearing assumption that task-solving skill and self-modification skill coincide (true only in coding): one unmodified loop improves Polyglot, paper review, Genesis reward design, and IMO grading, matching DGM where DGM is native and beating it everywhere else without per-domain handcrafting

Cleanest ablation design in the RSI literature: every run starts from the same deliberately trivial single-FM-call agent, and the fixed-meta (ADAS-replicating) and no-archive baselines isolate exactly how much comes from meta-level self-improvement and open-ended search rather than task-level optimization

Honest hard-to-verify evaluation: paper review scores agreement with observed human accept/reject decisions rather than claimed quality, and the E.5 experiment honestly reports that evolved parent selection loses to the handcrafted mechanism
limitations: Fixed task distribution: the paper's own first limitation — nothing co-evolves the tasks or curriculum, so 'any computable task' means any task a human has pre-defined an evaluator for

Full self-referentiality is deferred: parent selection and evaluation protocols stay handcrafted in the main experiments; the preliminary E.5 relaxation shows the agent reinvents UCB/softmax/stagnation heuristics but does not yet beat score-child-prop (0.491 vs 0.532, n.s.)

The headline meta-level wins over human engineering are median-only: DGM-H vs DGM-custom and the compounding gain (0.640 vs 0.610) are both not statistically significant, and the paper concedes saturation makes late gains small in absolute terms

Expensive and gate-sensitive: ~88.6M tokens per 100-iteration run (33M self-modification + 0.506M/iteration evaluation, App. D.2), and staged evaluation assigns zero to all unevaluated tasks of any agent failing a small-subset gate
2603.19461.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI, the direct generalization of DGM: the improver itself becomes improvable, and its improvements demonstrably transfer across domains (imp@50) and compound across runs. Read after DGM; pair with the HyperAgents repo card (the domains/ git-reset quarantine) and ADAS — which is exactly DGM-H w/o self-improve.
2603.19461.reading: §1–2 for the fixed-meta-layer critique and alignment assumption; §3 for hyperagents and metacognitive self-modification; §5.1–5.3 with Figures 2–4 (imp@50, transfer, compounding); §7 limitations; Appendix E.3 (learned memory/tracking) and E.5 (evolved parent selection).

2603.18000.tldr: AgentFactory keeps successful task solutions as executable Python subagents — not textual reflections — in a growing library, refines them from execution feedback, and re-exports them to other agent systems; saved subagents cut orchestrator output tokens roughly in half on transfer tasks.
2603.18000.method: A Meta-Agent orchestrates a three-tier skill system: fixed meta-skills (create_subagent, run_subagent, modify_subagent, list_saved_subagents, view_subagent_code, finish), fixed tool skills (Serper web_search, Jina web_reading, Playwright browser_automation, shell_command), and the one evolving tier — subagent skills saved as pure Python code plus a SKILL.md doc. Install: on an unsolved task the Meta-Agent decomposes it and builds a focused Python subagent per sub-problem, allocating each a tool subset rather than the whole toolset; on success the subagent is promoted from the isolated per-task workspace to the persistent library. Self-Evolve: on similar tasks it retrieves saved subagents, runs and assesses them, analyzes failure feedback, modifies the code (error handling, generality), and revalidates against the current task. Deploy: mature subagents export as standalone scripts; LangChain, AutoGen, and Claude Code onboard them via prompts + SKILL.md alone.
results: Table 1, Batch 2 transfer tasks with saved subagents, avg orchestrator output tokens/task: Opus 4.6 2971 vs ReAct 7022 (−58%) and 6210 for the textual-experience baseline; Sonnet 4.6 3862 vs ReAct 7029 (−45%) and 8223 textual

Stronger models reuse even without a pre-built library: Opus 4.6 already drops to 4324 tokens on Batch 1 from scratch vs ReAct 8298 (the paper flags this as a signal for future models); Sonnet 4.6 does not — 9199 vs ReAct 6893, i.e. building subagents from scratch cost more than plain ReAct

The metric isolates orchestration effort (subagent-internal LLM tokens excluded); setup is two 15-task batches where each Batch 2 task mirrors its Batch 1 counterpart with changed specifics, and all tasks completed without runtime errors in every configuration

Qualitative loops: a README-generation subagent evolves hardcoded path → LLM JSON parsing with fragile hardcoded fallback → LLM + regex fallback over three runs (Fig. 2); subagents created in AgentFactory (Audio Transcriber, Document Creator) are invoked directly inside Claude Code with no new subagent creation (Fig. 3)
advantages: Experience is executable: saved subagents re-run as code, so reuse replaces re-derivation — the Reflexion/STaR-style textual-experience baseline never approaches the Batch 2 savings (6210/8223 vs 2971/3862 tokens)
Cross-system portability is demonstrated, not just claimed: pure-Python subagents with SKILL.md docs (aligned to Anthropic's Agent Skills standard) onboarded into Claude Code via prompts alone

Improvement by accumulation under containment: meta- and tool-skills stay frozen while only the subagent tier evolves, and the Workspace Manager runs each task in isolation so failed modifications can't corrupt the shared library
limitations: The headline metric excludes subagent-internal token consumption — savings are orchestration-level only, and there is no output-quality score beyond 'all tasks completed without runtime errors' on 30 author-curated tasks
The from-scratch overhead is backbone-dependent: Sonnet 4.6's Batch 1 orchestration cost (9199) exceeds ReAct (6893); the paper's text highlights only the favorable Opus contrast (4324 vs 8298)
Interaction is web-only (search, reading, Playwright); the conclusion defers GUI/non-web applications to future VLM integration

Safety is by convention rather than guarantee: shell_command has built-in checks that flag destructive operations, and the ethical considerations section relies on human-readable code plus user auditing of exported subagents
2603.18000.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI (Self-Evolving Agent Frameworks): Voyager's code-as-skill lifted from single functions to whole subagents, with the paper's own ablation being Reflexion/STaR textual experience. Pairs with DGM (evolves the agent's internals rather than growing a capability library) and the stage-10 AgentFactory repo card for the implementation.
2603.18000.reading: Skim §3 for the three-phase lifecycle and skill tiers, §4 for both demonstrations (Fig. 2 path-resolution evolution, Fig. 3 Claude Code reuse), §5 + Table 1 for the token numbers, Appendix B for the 30 tasks.

2604.20133.tldr: EvoAgent wraps GPT5.2 in a user-feedback-driven dual loop — deterministic online skill matching/delegation, asynchronous offline skill extraction — lifting average LLM-as-Judge score 27.998% (3.547→4.541) in deployed foreign-trade use, while degrading weaker models.
2604.20133.method: A skill is the tuple (name, desc, triggers, instr, refs, meta): a multi-file package — SKILL.md plus lazily-loaded refs/ — carrying evolutionary metadata (usage count, success rate, timestamps). Online loop: three-stage cascading matching (case-insensitive trigger keywords → embedding cosine similarity above a 0.6 default threshold → LLM intent classification), structured context assembly, ReAct execution, and compression above 64K tokens that preserves an 'asset index' of skills, links, and key data; skills flagged requires_sub_agent spawn sub-agents with independent context spaces via OpenAI Agents SDK handoff, results flowing back past the main agent. Offline loop, triggered only at session end: an asynchronous Session Reviewer sub-agent updates SOUL.md/USER.md/MEMORY.md, extracts candidate skills, and grades maturity — Budding / Growing / Mature / Proficient at usage≥1 / ≥4 with success≥0.7 / ≥10 with success≥0.85. The MDP formalization is theoretical only: no numerical reward is computed; evolution runs on implicit usage/success statistics plus user feedback.
results: RQ1, five-dimension LLM-as-Judge (1–5 scale; 172 instances split from 20 sampled multi-turn dialogues out of 664 collected; queries script-generated over product category × target market × buyer type × 12 foreign-trade scenarios): GPT5.2 average 3.547 → 4.541 with EvoAgent (+27.998%); professionalism 2.703→4.762, accuracy 2.907→4.238, practicality 3.744→4.709, language quality 4.052→4.779, completeness flat 4.331→4.215 (−0.116)

RQ2 model transfer: GPT4.1 under EvoAgent drops ~13% below its own standalone baseline and reaches ~75% of EvoAgent-enhanced GPT5.2; Qwen3.5-35B-A3B drops to ~85% of standalone, 74.5% of enhanced GPT5.2 — the paper formalizes capability as γ1·inference + γ2·agent-implementation compatibility, conceding no ablations isolate the factors

RQ3 long-horizon memory: 420 dialogue turns with 6 compression events without runtime errors; no memory errors across 17 tests at 120 turns; full accuracy at 200 turns without compression; compression triggers when context exceeds 64K tokens
Latency: ~12s average response early, 14s around 80 turns, stabilizing at 24s beyond 120 turns; external tool calls add 5–30s depending on complexity
advantages: A concrete Harness Engineering instantiation (explicitly built on Hashimoto, OpenAI's Codex report, Böckeler/Fowler, Iusztin): deterministic low-latency online execution loop cleanly separated from an asynchronous offline evolution loop, compiling the MDP objective into post-session updates so no labeled data or numerical reward is needed

Full skill lifecycle modeled — generation, cascading matching, lazy-loading injection, maturity grading with explicit usage/success thresholds, pruning inputs — versus the implicit, unstructured capability updates it attributes to Voyager-style skill libraries

Publishes the negative transfer result most RSI papers omit: the same harness that gives GPT5.2 +27.998% degrades GPT4.1 ~13% and Qwen ~15%, evidence that architecture gains are a model–harness interaction, not a free amplifier
Deployed on a real foreign-trade assistant at Focus Technology rather than a benchmark; queries generated by a parameterized script independent of runtime skill-triggering outcomes
limitations: Paper's own, from the HarnessEngineering lens: evolution triggers only after session termination (unidirectional online→offline coupling) — 'delayed learning but not real-time adaptation' to skill degradation or intent shift
Only single-skill invocation per task — no multi-skill orchestration or parallel execution; user profiling relies on heuristic frequency thresholds; no cross-user knowledge sharing

Evaluation is small (172 instances), synthetic, and collected inside the deployed EvoAgent environment (authors concede distribution dependence); LLM-as-Judge scoring with no human validation, variance, or ablations; no head-to-head against a standalone-GPT compression/memory baseline
Compression irreversibly loses early dialogue details and long-term memory lacks automatic pruning; system lacks cost tracking, monitoring dashboards, and enterprise auth (JWT/OAuth)
2604.20133.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI: the industrial, user-in-the-loop counterpoint to EvoSkills' automated co-evolution verification (its main cited contrast) and Voyager's flat skill library. Pairs with RRSI and Harness-Zero on 'the harness moves scores' — and with the model–harness synergy caveat (GPT4.1/Qwen degradation) every RSI claim should be read against.
2604.20133.reading: §3.1–3.3 for the dual loop and skill tuple, §4.1–4.2 for the GPT5.2/GPT4.1/Qwen transfer numbers, §4.3.2 for the paper's own limitations; Appendix A pseudocode has exact matching and maturity thresholds.

2507.03616.tldr: EvoAgentX is an open-source platform unifying workflow generation, execution, evaluation, and evolution: TextGrad, MIPRO, SEW, and AFlow optimizers rewrite prompts, tool configs, and workflow graphs, gaining 7.44–10.00 points on HotPotQA/MBPP/MATH and up to 20.00% on GAIA.
2507.03616.method: Five layers: basic components (config/logging/checkpointing; LLMs via LiteLLM/OpenRouter), agent, workflow, evolving, evaluation. An agent is a ⟨LLM, memory, actions⟩ tuple; a workflow is a directed graph W=(V,E) of WorkFlowNodes carrying PENDING/RUNNING/COMPLETED/FAILED status — WorkFlowGraph for hand-built graphs, SequentialWorkFlowGraph inferring edges from task input/output dependencies. The evolving layer exposes three optimizer roles driven by evaluation feedback: an agent optimizer (TextGrad, MIPRO) rewriting prompt templates and tool configurations; a workflow optimizer (SEW, AFlow) restructuring the graph by reordering nodes, modifying dependencies, and trying alternative execution strategies; and a memory optimizer (under active development). The evaluation layer pairs task-specific metrics with an LLM-based evaluator, closing the run→score→update loop. In the AFlow demo config, each run allows 20 optimization rounds with 3 validation rounds, Claude 3.5 Sonnet as optimizer LLM and GPT-4o-mini as executor, over operators like Custom, CustomCodeGenerate, ScEnsemble.
results: Table 2, HotPotQA F1: 63.58 → 71.02 with TextGrad (AFlow 65.09, MIPRO 69.16); MATH solve rate: 66.00 → 76.00 with TextGrad (AFlow 71.00, MIPRO 72.30); MBPP pass@1: 69.00 → 79.00 with AFlow (TextGrad 71.00, MIPRO 68.00 — below the unoptimized baseline)
GAIA applications: Open Deep Research overall accuracy +18.41% (+20.00 Level 1, +8.71 Level 2, +7.69 Level 3); OWL +20.00% overall (+28.57 Level 1, +10.00 Level 2, +100.00 Level 3)
Built-in benchmark harness (Table 1): NQ, HotPotQA, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval (164), MBPP (427), LiveCodeBench v1–v5 (400–880 per version, plus 479 code-execution and 442 test-output-prediction items)

Case study (A.4): AFlow turns a one-prompt math workflow into a multi-agent pipeline (analysis → Python code generation → 3-sample ScEnsemble → answer formatting); TextGrad and MIPRO each expand a one-line boxed-answer prompt into structured step-by-step reasoning
advantages: Unified substrate where TextGrad, MIPRO, SEW, and AFlow optimize the same WorkFlowGraph representation over one shared benchmark harness — optimizers become swappable and head-to-head comparable (Table 2) rather than fragmented paper artifacts

Separates optimizer roles by what they touch — prompts/tool configs (agent) vs. graph topology (workflow) vs. memory — so agent-level and workflow-level evolution compose within one framework rather than competing designs
Optimizes other people's deployed systems, not just its own: prompt and topology refinement of Open Deep Research and OWL on GAIA
Evaluation is a first-class layer (task-specific metrics plus LLM-based evaluator) wired into the optimization loop, not a post-hoc script
limitations: The memory optimizer 'remains under active development' — Eq. 5 is aspirational, never demonstrated in the experiments
Table 2 reports single deltas against the unoptimized workflow with no ablations, variance, or cost/token accounting; on MBPP, MIPRO (68.00) lands below the 69.00 baseline, so optimization can hurt

The GAIA gains are level-relative percentages on two systems (OWL Level 3 '+100.00%') with no absolute accuracies or statistical treatment in the main text; the paper self-describes contributions as those of 'our demo'
Evolution is bounded by the integrated algorithms' search spaces (AFlow operators, SEW mutations) — the contribution is the harness, not a new evolution mechanism
2507.03616.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI: the runnable counterpart to the workflow-evolution papers it integrates (AFlow, SEW, TextGrad, MIPRO) — one graph representation, swappable optimizers. Its conclusion names MASS, AlphaEvolve, and Darwin Gödel Machine as future evolution strategies; read alongside those cards to move from reading workflow evolution to running it.
2507.03616.reading: Short paper: §3 (system design, especially §3.4 evolving layer), Table 2 and §4.1 for optimizer-by-benchmark numbers, §4.2 for GAIA, and Appendix A.4 for before/after workflow and prompt case studies.

2510.23601.tldr: Alita-G: a generalist agent self-evolves into a domain expert by generating, abstracting, and curating MCP tools.
2510.23601.method: A generalist agent runs a curation loop that generates, abstracts, and curates Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, transforming itself into a domain expert by accumulating reusable tools.
results: Self-generated MCP tools turn a generalist into a domain specialist, improving domain performance.
limitations: Tool quality is bounded by the generator; curation needs a feedback signal.
2510.23601.fits: Tool-creation as self-improvement — the agent extends itself by building the tools it needs (the MCP-native path).

2402.17574.tldr: Agent-Pro evolves an LLM agent's behavioral policy — its prompt-level beliefs and decision rules — through in-game reflection and payoff-based selection, letting GPT-4 beat the trained DMC poker bot in Limit Texas Hold'em with zero parameter updates.
2402.17574.method: Policy here means the prompt itself: task description plus behavioral strategy. 'Training' is gradient-free prompt optimization through play. Each decision, the agent first writes natural-language beliefs — self-belief (hand, plan, risk) and world-belief (opponents, rules) — then acts conditioned on them. After lost games, policy-level reflection audits the whole belief sequence against the delayed final result (correctness, consistency, rationality), not single actions, and distills failures into two instruction types: Behavioral Guidelines (goals, strategies, demonstration trajectories) and World Modeling (opponent models, overlooked rules). New instructions are verified by replaying the same game (kept only if the score improves, ≤3 retries), then evaluated on novel games with all hands and seats swapped across (K+1)² permutations; the metric Δ is the average margin over the strongest opponent. A depth-first search over B=8 candidate policies per iteration accepts any Δ gain and backtracks otherwise — in-context policy iteration.
results: Blackjack, 900 games vs dealer (Table 1): win rate 36.2% on Qwen-72B (+3.9 over best baseline Reflexion 32.3), 23.1% on Llama2-70B (+11.0 over Reflexion's 12.1), 38.2% on GPT-3.5 (+1.5); on GPT-4 it reaches 40.4%, 0.5 below plain ReAct (40.9). Paper's overall claim: ~+4% average advantage; GPT-3.5 Agent-Pro tops the human reference (37.1%, Table C3).

Limit Hold'em, 1600 test games (Table 2), GPT-4 base: Agent-Pro averages 4.3 chips per game vs Vanilla LLM 1.4 (+2.9), beating the trained DMC bot (1.1, +3.2), ReAct (2.2) and Reflexion (1.2); human reference 5.7. GPT-3.5 base: 1.2 vs −1.1 (+2.3); Llama2-70B: −1.4 vs −2.2 (+0.8) — average gain ~+2 chips.

Ablations on GPT-4 (Table B2): belief-aware decisions alone (no learning) score 2.7 chips (+1.3 over vanilla); reflection without the belief module drops to 2.5 and yields vague, verbose instructions — beliefs help both deciding and reflecting.

Few-shot demonstration does not substitute for evolution: adding 3 winning example hands to the vanilla prompt scores 0.9 chips (−0.5), 3 losing hands 2.0 (+0.6), both far below the evolved policy's 4.3.

Learned styles diverge by base model when dealt the same bad hand: GPT-4-based Agent-Pro bluffs and probes, GPT-3.5 plays cautiously and folds late, Llama2-70B collapses into folding at the start (§5.2, Fig 4-5).
advantages: Shifts reflection from the action level to the policy level: it checks belief trajectories against delayed, game-level outcomes and compiles them into reusable instructions, which is exactly where action-level correction (Reflexion) stalls in long-horizon zero-sum play — e.g. Llama2-70B Blackjack 23.1% vs 12.1%.

Verification-plus-swap evaluation is a genuine in-context analog of policy iteration: a new prompt is accepted only when Δ improves on novel games with hands and seats permuted (K+1)² times, making gains luck-free and monotonic without any gradient step.

Shows strategic behaviors — bluffing, disguising strength, cutting losses — emerging purely from reflection on ~167 curated losing hands, and demonstrates that winning demonstrations are useless as prompts while failures drive reflection.
Ablates its own load-bearing parts: the dynamic belief module improves decisions even without learning (+1.3 chips) and is also necessary for high-quality reflection (4.3 → 2.5 without it).
limitations: Paper's own: heavy dependency on the base model — the GPT-4-based agent nears human level and beats DMC, but GPT-3.5 and Llama2-70B versions remain below DMC despite notable gains.
Paper's own: a significant gap likely remains to state-of-the-art game algorithms such as CFR+; no head-to-head against such solvers is run.
Evidence covers only two RLCard card games; Blackjack learning is simplified (50 failed games, no verification or DFS), and Hold'em evaluation rests on 100 test hands × 16 permutations.
On the simpler game the ceiling shows: with GPT-4, Agent-Pro (40.4%) does not beat plain ReAct (40.9%) at Blackjack, and the paper notes different strategies perform 'quite similarly' there.
2402.17574.fits: Moves self-evolution from prompt tweaks to the decision layer: the evolving artifact is a behavioral policy — beliefs plus decision rules — verified and selected by in-game payoff, i.e. gradient-free policy iteration for LLM agents (stage 5, harness-level). A direct precursor to policy-level RL-agent evolution, and an early case of LLM-judged evolution beating trained RL opponents.
2402.17574.reading: §3 (belief-aware decisions 3.1, policy-level reflection 3.2, DFS evolution 3.3), §4-5 results with Tables 1-2 and B2, the Limitations paragraphs; Appendix A.3-A.4 for the 50/167-hand setups and Table C3 for RL/human reference.

2409.00872.tldr: A training-free three-agent loop (User/Assistant/Checker) plus Ebbinghaus-style MemorySyntax memory management roughly doubles Reflexion's long-context QA F1 and yields up to 2.26x AgentBench gains, with the largest improvements on the smallest models.
2409.00872.method: Three roles: a User supplies the task description d_U and reference instance i_U; an Assistant samples outputs o_t ~ pi_theta(o_t | s_t, R_t, f_t); a Checker compares each output to the expected result and returns feedback f_t, looping until the Checker validates or an iteration cap N is hit. Two memories: STM keeps the recent trajectory (o_t, a_t); LTM accumulates reflections r_t = ref(o_1:t, R_1:t) — insight text over sparse binary rewards — appended via M^L <- M^L U {r_t}. MemorySyntax scores each item's retention R(I_t, tau) = e^(-tau/S) with strength S tied to information entropy; a linguistic rewriter produces I*_t with raised strength, then thresholds theta1 > theta2 gate three outcomes: keep in STM (R >= theta1), promote to LTM (theta2 <= R < theta1), discard (R < theta2). Despite policy-gradient-flavored formalism, the implementation is prompt-level with no weight updates.
results: AgentBench (6 tasks): GPT-3.5 Database 15.7 -> 35.6 (the abstract's 2.26x headline); Qwen-7B KG 0.0 -> 48.0; ChatGLM2-6B OS 0.0 -> 15.2; claimed relative gains of 57.7%-100% across five open-source models.
Multi-task evaluation: HotpotQA answer accuracy GPT-3.5 54.1% -> 74.9% (+20.8) and GPT-4 61.2% -> 78.4% (+17.2); Mistral-7b ALFWorld step completion 56.5% -> 73.8% (+17.3).

Head-to-head on long-context tasks vs Reflexion and Beam Search: HotpotQA F1 22.06 vs 11.26/10.26 and TriviaQA F1 22.76 vs 11.23/12.13 (roughly 2x), while code completion is near-parity (LCC F1 79.29 vs 79.28/79.12; RepoBench-P 81.22 vs 80.25/79.87).
RAG comparison: beats Fusion-in-Decoder on HotpotQA 74.8 vs 70.1 (+4.7), Natural Questions 73.6 (+3.8), TriviaQA 75.5 (+3.6), cutting memory 456 -> 231 MB (-50%) at similar latency.
Ablation (memory optimization on/off): CodeLlama-7B DB 2.7 -> 41.3 and WS 14.3 -> 58.7; Qwen-1.8B KG 6.8 -> 45.3 and ALF 0.0 -> 10.5.
advantages: The same reflection-plus-memory recipe lifts both API models and 1.8-7B open models with zero training: Qwen-1.8B goes from near-floor (2.7 OS, 0.6 M2W) to 18.7/13.6, approaching GPT-3.5 on several AgentBench tasks — the strongest evidence that harness-level memory/reflection can substitute for scale.

On long multi-document QA, structured memory management roughly doubles Reflexion's F1 (11.26 -> 22.06 HotpotQA; 11.23 -> 22.76 TriviaQA), isolating the memory-lifecycle contribution beyond Reflexion's verbal retry.

MemorySyntax replaces FIFO eviction (MemGPT) and time-only decay (MemoryBank) with an entropy-strength score plus a three-way retain/promote/discard threshold gate, and measurably cuts RAG memory footprint ~50%.
Error analysis ties the mechanism to concrete failure modes: Context-Limit-Exceeded and invalid-format errors are nearly eliminated on OS/DB tasks, with invalid-action errors reduced.
limitations: No limitations section, no variance or significance reported, and numbers are internally inconsistent: Table 5's 'with memory' CodeLlama-7B KG/WS scores (48.0/58.7) exceed Table 1's SAGE values for the same model/tasks (27.0/40.2).

The Checker derives feedback from the expected output of the reference instance i_U, so the loop presumes an available ground truth; thresholds theta1/theta2, the iteration cap N, and retention parameters are never assigned values in the paper.

The Nash-equilibrium convergence theorem (Thm 3.1) assumes policy-gradient and convex-optimization updates on compact strategy spaces, while the system is explicitly training-free prompting — the formalism is not connected to the actual mechanism.

Iterative checker loops cost wall-clock time: the paper's own Table 6 shows SAGE-ChatGPT-4 at 10.6-10.9 min per task vs 6.5-8.7 for BabyAGI/AutoGPT/HuggingGPT/LangChain/TaskMatrix.AI, unremarked despite the RAG section's 'without increasing latency' claim.
2409.00872.fits: A Harness-level RSI entry that is an explicit hybrid of stage-3 reflection (Reflexion-style verbal self-critiques written to long-term memory) and stage-4 memory (MemoryBank's Ebbinghaus decay, hardened into a three-way retain/promote/discard gate), all wrapped in a Checker-driven iteration loop. Adds multi-agent feedback and error-rate reduction rather than single-agent retry; pairs with Reflexion and MemoryBank as their synthesis.
2409.00872.reading: Read Sec 3.1-3.2 (checker loop, reflection, MemorySyntax), then Tables 1-3 (AgentBench, HotpotQA/MultiWOZ/ALFWorld, Reflexion comparison) and the Table 5 ablation. Appendix A is formal game theory — skimmable.

2305.19118.tldr: Names and measures the Degeneration-of-Thought (DoT) failure of single-agent self-reflection — confidence locks in wrong answers — and fixes it with Multi-Agent Debate (MAD): two 'tit-for-tat' debaters plus a judge with adaptive break, lifting GPT-3.5-Turbo past GPT-4 on commonsense MT.
2305.19118.method: The paper names DoT: once an LLM is confident in an answer, self-reflection stops generating novel thoughts even when the initial stance is wrong, quantified as adjacent-iteration opposition over 5 forced rounds (Fig. 1): self-reflection's disagreement stays low while debate keeps it high. MAD runs three agents: an affirmative debater, a negative debater prompted to 'disagree with the affirmative side's points', and a judge. Debaters speak in fixed order, each conditioned on the full debate history H. The judge has two modes: discriminative (is a correct solution on the table? True ends the debate early, the adaptive break) and extractive (pull the final answer from H at the iteration limit, set to 3). All roles share one backbone LLM (vicuna-7b/13b-v1.5-16k, GPT-3.5-Turbo-0301, GPT-4-0314), zero-shot at temperature 0; tasks are Common MT (Chinese⇒English commonsense ambiguity) and the authors' 200-question Counter-Intuitive AR set.
results: Common MT human direct assessment (1-5), GPT-3.5-Turbo baseline → +MAD vs GPT-4: lexical 3.14 → 3.78 (GPT-4 3.41), contextless 3.43 → 3.67 (3.63), contextual 3.57 → 3.67 (3.65) — MAD on Turbo beats GPT-4 on all three, and on COMET/BLEURT it matches or edges GPT-4 (contextual COMET 85.3 vs 85.0); Self-Reflect reaches only 3.43 lexical
Counter-Intuitive AR accuracy: 26.0% (Turbo) → 37.0% with MAD, vs Self-Reflect 27.5%, CoT 28.0%, Self-Consistency 29.5%; GPT-4 stays ahead at 51.0%
DoT mitigation vs Self-Reflect: human-labeled ambiguity-error (bias) 29.0 → 24.8 and output diversity (100 - Self-BLEU) 19.3 → 49.7
Math/symbolic transfer (Turbo, Appendix C): MAD vs CoT — GSM8K 73.8 vs 70.2, AddSub 92.1 vs 87.3, BBH Date 65.2 vs 56.4, Penguin 63.7 vs 58.9; cost 2.46x CoT's generated tokens (Self-Reflect 1.83x)

Ablations (Sec 4): debater quality dominates judge quality (Turbo debaters: 3.47 HUMAN with a vicuna-13b judge vs 3.69 with a Turbo judge); the judge favors its own backbone (GPT-4 judging GPT-4-vs-Turbo picks the GPT-4 side 120/200 vs 77); more debaters hurt (2 → 3 → 4: COMET 84.4 → 83.1 → 82.9); modest level-2 'tit for tat' beats full consensus (HUMAN 3.00 → 3.81) and forced total disagreement (0.988 disagreement, 3.72)
advantages: First to name and operationally measure DoT (adjacent-iteration disagreement), turning 'self-reflection plateaus' into a diagnosable failure with a causal account — bias, rigidity, missing external feedback — each mapped to a mechanism of the fix
Divergence by construction rather than hope: the negative debater is instructed to oppose, so the loop cannot quietly agree with itself the way Self-Reflect does (diversity 49.7 vs 19.3)
The judge's adaptive break ends most debates after one round and outperforms forcing any fixed iteration count (Fig. 5), keeping overhead at 2.46x CoT tokens

Reports the negative results later debate work leans on — adding debaters hurts, forced disagreement backfires, LLM judges favor their own backbone — and states the mitigations (modest tit-for-tat, one LLM for all roles) in the limitations
limitations: Time/compute cost of multi-round interaction: 2.46x CoT's generated tokens on Counter-Intuitive AR, vs 1.83x for Self-Reflect (Sec. Limitations, Appendix E)
Long-context degradation: with more debaters, 'LLM-based debaters tend to forget the views of other debaters' and judge extraction degrades — 2 debaters beat 3 and 4 (Table 7)
LLM judges are not impartial across backbones (self-preference, Table 6); the authors recommend identical LLMs for judge and debaters
Counter-Intuitive AR is the authors' own 200-question set (elicitation questionnaires + web puzzles), and MAD does not close the gap to GPT-4 there (37.0 vs 51.0)
2305.19118.fits: Stage 6: the diagnostic companion to Du et al.'s debate paper (2305.14325) — debate instrumented against self-reflection with a named failure mode (DoT) and a judge-plus-adaptive-break control loop. Its 'other agents beat self-feedback' argument underwrites the multi-agent arc toward debate-generated training data; pair with Reflexion as the single-agent foil.
2305.19118.reading: Sec 1-2 (DoT definition, MAD loop, judge modes), Table 1 + Sec 3.3 (Turbo+MAD vs GPT-4), Table 3 (CIAR), Sec 4.1-4.3 (DoT mitigation, judge fairness, tit-for-tat levels), Table 12 (token cost).

2305.14325.tldr: Having multiple LLM instances propose, critique, and revise answers over debate rounds reliably beats single-agent generation and self-reflection — e.g. GSM8K 77.0 to 85.0% — and the resulting debate transcripts can be distilled back, creating a model self-improvement loop.
2305.14325.method: Multiple copies of gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 independently answer the same prompt (zero-shot chain-of-thought) — only black-box generations, no weights or likelihoods. Each debate round, every agent receives the other agents' full responses concatenated as context plus a consensus prompt ("using the solutions from other agents as additional information, can you provide your answer?") and revises. Main configuration: 3 agents, 2 rounds; accuracy rises monotonically with agents and rounds (gains plateau past 4 rounds; 5+ agents need peers' responses summarized to fit context). "Stubborn" long-form prompts slow consensus and improve final answers; convergence is not guaranteed (debate is a multi-agent game) but agents almost always settle on one shared answer. Unlike majority voting, the model itself integrates the responses.
results: Arithmetic: 81.8±2.3% vs 67.0±4.7% single agent; self-reflection 72.1%, majority voting only 69.0% (3 agents, 2 rounds)
GSM8K: 85.0±3.5% vs 77.0±4.2% single agent (majority voting 81.0%); helps with and without zero-shot CoT
Chess move optimality (Stockfish pawn-score delta): 122.9±7.6 vs 91.4±10.6 single agent
Factuality: new 524-computer-scientist biography benchmark 73.8±2.3 vs 66.0±2.2; MMLU 71.1±4.6 vs 63.9 single — self-reflection drops MMLU to 57.7; chess move validity 45.2 vs 29.3
chatGPT+Bard debate solves 17/20 GSM8K vs 14 (chatGPT) and 11 (Bard) alone; persona initialization lifts MMLU 71.1 to 74.2
advantages: Makes debate between model copies a practical inference-time gain on black-box APIs: identical prompts and procedure across all six tasks, no gradient or likelihood access
Beats majority voting (the model integrates answers rather than tallying them) and peer critique beats self-reflection — which actually hurt factuality on MMLU (57.7 vs 63.9)

Not just answer amplification: many cases show all agents initially wrong yet converging on the correct answer; agents disagree on uncertain facts and drop them, and ease of persuasion may itself signal factual confidence
Explicitly frames debate transcripts as training data to distill back into the base model — a self-improvement loop — and introduces the biography factuality benchmark
limitations: Computationally expensive: every round needs a full generation per agent, multiplying cost (paper's own §5), though framed as data generation for distillation
Convergence is not correctness: debates settle on single answers that can be wrong while agents confidently affirm them — models cannot express uncertainty, so shared errors survive (§5)
Long debates overflow attention: models "only focused on the most recent generations" of a long debate history
Small eval sets (~100 problems per task) and the biography metric uses chatGPT itself as judge; agents' agreeableness may be an artifact of RLHF instruction tuning
2305.14325.fits: The canonical multi-agent debate paper — the social, quorum-based alternative to single-model self-correction at stage 6. Pairs with the Divergent Thinking paper (2305.19118): that motivates why diverse self-attempts help, this supplies the consensus mechanism later RSI pipelines reuse to generate training data.
2305.14325.reading: Sections 2.1–2.2 (protocol, prompt-controlled consensus), Tables 1–2 with Figure 10 (agents/rounds scaling), and §5 Limitations; Figure 3 plus §3.3 for short vs long debate prompts.

2511.16043.tldr: Agent0 evolves math-reasoning agents from zero human data by co-evolving two RL-trained agents — a curriculum generator rewarded for frontier-difficulty, tool-heavy tasks and a tool-using executor trained on majority-vote pseudo-labels — lifting Qwen3-8B-Base 18% on math and 24% on general reasoning.
2511.16043.method: From one base LLM (Qwen3-4B/8B-Base), Agent0 clones two agents and alternates GRPO training over 3 iterations. Curriculum agent: generates tasks under reward RC = Rformat·max(0, λunc·Runc + λtool·Rtool − Rrep), where Runc = 1−2|p̂−0.5| peaks when the executor's self-consistency over k=10 sampled solutions is 50% (frontier difficulty), Rtool = γ·min(Ntool, 4) counts code-execution calls in executor responses, and Rrep penalizes BLEU-clustered duplicate tasks. Executor: the frozen curriculum agent emits a task pool; tasks in the intermediate self-consistency band (|p̂−0.5| ≤ δ, δ=0.25) are kept, the majority vote becomes the pseudo-label, and training uses ADPO — advantages scaled down on low-consistency (noisy-label) tasks while the upper clip is relaxed there so low-probability tokens (new reasoning paths) can grow. Rollouts are multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning: generation pauses at python code blocks, a sandbox returns the output, looping until a boxed answer.
results: Qwen3-8B-Base, math AVG (AMC/MATH/GSM8K/Olympiad/Minerva/AIME24-25): 49.2 → 58.2 (+18%); AIME24 13.9 → 28.0, AIME25 16.7 → 24.8, Minerva 50.0 → 61.3. General benchmarks: MMLU-Pro 51.8 → 63.4, SuperGPQA 28.3 → 33.0, BBEH 8.6 → 13.7 (abstract's +24% is the relative gain across the three general benchmarks; Table 2 'Overall AVG' 34.5 → 42.1 includes math).

Beats data-free baselines on 8B math AVG: 58.2 vs R-Zero 54.7 (+6.4%), Absolute Zero 52.6 (+10.6%), Socratic-Zero 56.1 (+3.7%) — the last despite Socratic-Zero relying on external OpenAI APIs; the base model given the tool zero-shot only reaches 53.2.
Qwen3-4B-Base: math AVG 42.6 → 52.5; general Overall AVG 27.1 → 37.6 (SuperGPQA 20.9 → 29.9, MMLU-Pro 37.4 → 55.9, BBEH 7.57 → 12.0).

Co-evolution is measurable: the frozen Iter-1 executor's pass rate on curricula from iterations 1/2/3 falls 64.0% → 58.5% → 51.0% while average tool calls rise 1.65 → 2.10 → 2.60; 8B math AVG climbs 55.1 → 56.5 → 58.2 across the three iterations.

Ablations (8B math AVG, full Agent0 = 58.2): 46.8 without curriculum-agent training, 48.7 without the tool reward, 47.9 without the repetition penalty, 56.2 with vanilla GRPO instead of ADPO, 55.9 without multi-turn; 4-turn vs 1-turn curriculum generation adds 3.4% overall.
advantages: Genuinely zero human data: both agents start from the same base model, and tasks, pseudo-labels (executor majority vote), and training rewards (uncertainty, tool use) are all self-generated — no external corpus or annotations enter training.

Breaks the self-play capability ceiling the paper identifies in prior work: difficulty targeting (p̂ ≈ 0.5) plus an explicit tool-use reward measurably escalates task complexity iteration over iteration (Table 5) instead of stagnating at the base model's level.
ADPO tackles the pseudo-label noise inherent to self-play RL head-on: ambiguity-scaled advantages plus dynamic trust regions beat vanilla GRPO by 2 math points (58.2 vs 56.2).
limitations: Pseudo-labels are majority votes, so label noise on ambiguous tasks is inherent; ADPO only downweights unreliable signals rather than eliminating them (the paper's own motivation for ambiguity-aware scaling).

The paper concedes that closed-loop self-evolution without the external tool 'risks mode collapse and curriculum stagnation' because it is bounded by the model's inherent knowledge — the sandboxed code interpreter is load-bearing.

The curriculum prompt casts the generator as a competition-math problem setter; coverage beyond math is shown only as transfer to three general benchmarks, on Qwen3-4B/8B-Base alone, and the paper is labeled 'preliminary work'.

The pipeline is data-free but not external-model-free: Appendix A uses a GPT-4o answer-checking judge (temperature 0.1); compute demand is heavy (k=10 executor samples per task for both curriculum reward and pseudo-labels, 16 rollout groups, multi-turn sandbox calls), though the paper reports no GPU budget.
2511.16043.fits: The zero-human-data extreme of stage-6 multi-agent self-improvement: a curriculum/executor symbiosis in the Absolute Zero / R-Zero / Socratic-Zero lineage, distinguished by putting tool-integrated reasoning inside the loop so task complexity ratchets past the base model's ceiling instead of stagnating.
2511.16043.reading: §3 for the curriculum reward (Eqs. 2–5), frontier filtering (Eq. 7), and ADPO (§3.3.2); then §4.2 Tables 1–2, §4.3 Tables 3 and 5 (difficulty/tool-use escalation); Appendix A for hyperparameters and prompts.

2406.14228.tldr: EvoAgent treats any existing LLM agent as a parent whose role/skill/prompt settings form an evolvable genome, and applies LLM-simulated crossover, mutation, and quality-checked selection to grow it into a specialized multi-agent team that beats hand-designed multi-agent frameworks on reasoning, science, and planning benchmarks.
2406.14228.method: An individual is one agent from any framework; its evolvable genome is its natural-language settings (role, skills, prompts), so LLMs can simulate the operators by rewriting them. From initial parent A(0,0), each of T iterations runs: (1) Crossover — parents answer the query, an LLM inspects the results to pick skills to improve, and rewrites settings into child agents; (2) Mutation — an LLM compares children against parents and edits them until distinct yet still task-capable; (3) Selection — an LLM quality-check module discards children that fail to inherit parent characteristics or duplicate an existing skill type (Fig. 1's hotel agent is dropped for duplicating the accommodation agent), keeping N per iteration; (4) Result update — every survivor drafts an answer and an LLM integrates all candidates with the prior result (EvoUpdate). All earlier agents stay in the population (EvoAgent(N,T) yields N×T specialists per query; main runs are (1,3)).
results: Logic Grid Puzzle (200 puzzles, accuracy): GPT-4 77.0 vs hand-designed AutoAgents 69.0, AgentVerse 66.5, CoT 65.5; GPT-3.5 71.5 vs 68.0/66.5; Llama2-13B 35.5 vs Self-Refine 33.5 while persona-ensemble SPP collapses to 0.0 (Table 1).

TravelPlanner (180-query validation, GPT-4): final macro pass rate 7.2 vs 2.2 Direct/CoT, 1.1 Self-Refine, 0.6 SPP; hard-constraint micro 21.1 vs 15.8; commonsense micro 81.5 vs 79.4. On Mistral-7B it doubles hard-constraint micro (7.8 vs 3.9) and is the only method with nonzero final pass (1.1 vs 0.0).

ScienceWorld (30 interactive science tasks, sub-task completion): GPT-4 overall 27.97 to 30.42 and GPT-3.5 17.12 to 19.02 over the single-agent ReAct baseline; biggest gains on short trajectories (GPT-4 42.41 to 48.67), smallest on long ones (Table 2).

Ablation (TravelPlanner, averaged GPT-3.5 + Gemini-Pro): EvoAgent(1,3) with quality check reaches 68.9 commonsense / 14.0 hard micro vs same-budget variants Overgen3 61.4/10.7, PromptRefine3 63.0/13.8, Suggest3 61.7/8.4, Direct 59.5/13.7 (Table 4).

Cost (Table 5, Llama-3.1-70B on 8x RTX 3090 via SGLang): Logic 67.0 in 1060.8s vs AutoAgents 61.5 in 988.8s and AgentVerse 60.0 in 1056.0s — near-identical wall-clock to other multi-agent baselines at the best score. The MetaGPT/CAMEL/AutoGen adaptations (Appendix D) report no benchmark numbers — qualitative demos only.
advantages: Framework-agnostic by construction: because the genome is plain-language agent settings, the same four operators wrap MetaGPT, AutoGen, and CAMEL without modifying their code — unlike ADAS (stage 5), which must program a new executable pipeline per domain and framework.

Selection needs no validation metric: the quality check tests inheritance and non-duplication rather than benchmark fitness, so the loop runs on tasks where you cannot score candidates individually (at the cost of optimizer signal — see limitations).

Gains hold on weak backbones where persona methods fail: on Llama2-13B Logic it scores 35.5 while SPP scores 0.0, showing diversity-from-evolution generalizes where SPP's persona self-collaboration does not.

Outperforms the dedicated auto-generation frameworks AgentVerse and AutoAgents it is closest to, at comparable inference cost, and beats same-budget ablations (Overgen, PromptRefine, Suggest), isolating the value of evolving agents rather than just sampling or refining prompts.
limitations: From the paper's own Limitations section: generating multiple specialized agents brings higher token cost than a single agent; comparisons with existing multi-agent frameworks are limited to AgentVerse and AutoAgents because adapting others to each benchmark was out of scope; and the generated agents' quality is never manually evaluated.
Improvements shrink as trajectories lengthen — ScienceWorld gains are largest on short tasks and the authors attribute this to long contexts degrading multi-agent systems (Table 2).

Iteration gains plateau after 3 on Trivia Creative Writing as generated agents converge and become similar, and with N>1 the quality-check module is needed to suppress duplicate-type agents (Sec. 4.4, App. B).
Scaling population/iterations shifts plans toward user preferences at the expense of commonsense-rule adherence — the authors blame an initial-agent integration bias they leave to future work.
2406.14228.fits: Stage 6: ADAS-style evolutionary search pointed at multi-agent societies. Adds over ADAS (stage 5): the search space is language-level role/prompt settings inside any existing framework (MetaGPT/AutoGen/CAMEL wrap-in), not new forward() code, and selection is an LLM inheritance/diversity check instead of a scored archive — wider plug-in reach, weaker optimization signal. Predates ADAS (June 2024).
2406.14228.reading: Sec. 3 plus Algorithm 1 for the four operators; Tables 1 and 3 for the headline numbers; Sec. 4.4 ablations; Appendix D only to see framework wrap-in (qualitative); Limitations. Skip the prompt listings.

2403.08715.tldr: Behavior cloning plus self-reinforcement on GPT-4-rated social interactions lifts Mistral-7B to GPT-4-level social goal completion on SOTOPIA (7.62 vs 7.62), improves safety, preserves MMLU — while revealing GPT-4 judges overestimate agents trained on GPT-4 ratings.
2403.08715.method: Three automated steps. (1) Task generation: GPT-4 turns keywords sampled from Social Chemistry, Social IQa, and Normbank into scenarios with paired private goals (462 tasks from 510 prompts), reusing SOTOPIA's 40 character profiles — unfiltered, disjoint from eval tasks. (2) Data collection: behavior cloning (BC) data comes from GPT-4-agent vs GPT-4-agent interactions; self-reinforcement (SR) data from the Mistral-7B agent role-playing both characters — 100 tasks × 10 character-pair interactions per round. (3) Update: GPT-4 rates each agent's goal completion (0-10, the best human-correlated SOTOPIA-EVAL dimension). BC keeps the top-2 interactions per task per agent plus a rank-wise min(local, global) mean threshold; SR keeps the top 20% per task (ratio-based, replacing ReST's iteratively tuned thresholds). Filtered positive (context, history) → JSON-action pairs train Mistral-7B-Instruct via QLoRA SFT, sequentially BC then SR.
results: GPT-4-judged goal completion on SOTOPIA-hard: base Mistral-7B 3.25 → BC+SR 5.71, near the GPT-4 expert's 5.89; on all 90 tasks 5.07 → 7.62, exactly matching GPT-4's 7.62 (overall 2.33 → 3.44 vs GPT-4's 3.31).
Human evaluation is weaker: hard-task goal completion 2.89 (base) → 4.29 (BC+SR) vs GPT-4's 5.25; overall 1.04 → 1.95 (BC+SR vs GPT-4's 2.07, not significant, p=0.355).
The GPT-4-vs-human goal-score gap on hard tasks grows from 0.36 (base) to 1.42 (BC+SR): optimizing the LLM rating widens judge–human divergence.
Beyond goal completion (human, hard tasks), BC+SR over base: believability +2.05, relationship +1.91, social rules +1.11, overall +0.91 (all significant); knowledge −0.14, secret 0.00.

MMLU 5-shot preserved: BC+SR 48.57 vs base 49.21 (SR alone drops to 43.46). On a violence-refusal task, BC+SR's proceed-to-injure rate falls 100% → 44% (matching GPT-4), toxic words 3.6 → 0.9 (GPT-4: 0.3), and as the persuader character it prevents injury 11% → 100% with 2.9 alternative solutions vs GPT-4's 1.2.
advantages: Runs the BC + LLM-rated self-reinforcement recipe (ReST-style) on open-ended multi-turn social interaction — private goals, secrets, non-verbal actions — rather than Stable Alignment's single-turn QA, and a 7B model reaches the GPT-4 expert's goal-completion score under the same judge.

Ratio-based filtering (top 20% per task) removes ReST's iterative threshold tuning, enabling single-pass SR across tasks of mixed difficulty; one round of BC alone already surpasses the GPT-3.5-based agent (goal 4.82 vs 4.21, auto-rated hard tasks).

Side benefits without explicit alignment training: safety and toxicity improve on their probe task and MMLU is preserved, suggesting social-interaction skill is roughly orthogonal to general QA ability.

Documents reward hacking inside its own loop: training on GPT-4 ratings inflates GPT-4-judged scores faster than human scores — a concrete warning for any self-improvement pipeline that uses an LLM as its own reward.
limitations: Headline parity holds only under GPT-4 judging; by human rating BC+SR stays below GPT-4 (4.29 vs 5.25 goal completion on hard tasks) and the judge–human gap grows 0.36 → 1.42 (the paper's own central caveat).
The method is offline and single-pass — no online RL or iteration (PPO left to future work); the expert is GPT-4, and human conversation data as a BC source is deferred.
Safety conclusions rest on a single custom social task (paper acknowledges); trained models still emit more toxic words than GPT-4 (0.9 vs 0.3), and SR alone degrades MMLU (43.46 vs 49.21).
Training tasks are auto-generated and deliberately unfiltered ('lower quality'), and human evaluation covers only 28 interactions per model on the 14 hard scenarios.
2403.08715.fits: Extends self-improvement to the social dimension stage-6 multi-agent settings exercise: open-ended multi-turn role-play with private goals, secrets, and non-verbal acts. Its LLM-rater-as-reward + filtered self-training loop is self-play data curation for social skills — and the judge-vs-human divergence result is direct evidence of reward hacking in LLM-judged self-improvement.
2403.08715.reading: §2.1 (SOTOPIA-EVAL dimensions), §3 (pipeline + filtering), §5 with Fig 4 and Tables 1-2, §6 (safety, MMLU); Appendix B.2 for exact filtering rules and Table 5 for full per-dimension numbers.

2412.21139.tldr: SWE-Gym: the first *training environment* for software-engineering agents — 2,438 real Python tasks with runtime + tests — used to train agents and verifiers.
2412.21139.method: First training environment for SWE agents: 2,438 real-world Python task instances (codebase + executable runtime + unit tests + NL task); used to RL-train agents and inference-time verifiers.
results: Trained agents gain up to +19% absolute on SWE-Bench Verified/Lite; verifiers add inference-time scaling.

2412.21139.reading: Read the environment design (§3) and the training results (§4–5).

2304.05128.tldr: Self-Debug: teach the LLM to debug its own code — explain the program, then generate a fix — via few-shot demonstrations.
2304.05128.method: Few-shot demonstrations teach the LLM to debug its predicted program by explaining the code, then generating a fix; optionally uses execution results (traceback) as extra signal.
results: Large gains on code generation (e.g., up to ~12%+ on Text-to-SQL, TransCoder, MBPP) without training.
limitations: Improvement depends on the debugging demonstrations; gains vary by task.
2304.05128.fits: The code-domain instantiation of Self-Refine — self-correction applied to programs, with execution as optional ground truth.
2304.05128.reading: Read the explain-then-fix loop (§3) and the execution-feedback variant.

2312.13010.tldr: AgentCoder splits code generation into three roles — a Chain-of-Thought programmer, a test designer that writes basic/edge/large-scale tests without seeing the code, and a Python test-executor — looping until tests pass. GPT-4 reaches 96.3% HumanEval pass@1 at 56.9K tokens.
2312.13010.method: Input is only the task description/stub. The programmer agent (LLM) emits code after a four-step Chain-of-Thought (understand and clarify, select algorithm, write pseudocode, generate code). The test designer agent (LLM, separate call) emits test cases independently — it sees the prompt stub but never the generated code, so its oracles cannot be biased by the bugs it is meant to catch — and is prompted for basic, edge, and large-scale inputs. The test executor agent is a Python script, not an LLM: agents must wrap output in ```py[Code]```/```py[TestCases]``` blocks, which it extracts, runs in a local terminal, and inspects for assertion/runtime errors. All tests pass → return code; otherwise the traceback is fed to the programmer, which regenerates. Loop ends on success or at an iteration budget (5 in experiments). Nothing is trained — all improvement is in-context repair.
results: GPT-4: 96.3% HumanEval / 91.8% MBPP pass@1 at 56.9K/66.3K response tokens, vs MetaGPT 85.9/87.7 at 138.2K/206.5K, ChatDev 84.1/79.8 at 183.7K/259.3K, AgentVerse 89.0/73.5 at 149.2K/193.6K, Self-Collaboration 90.2/78.9 at 74.3K/89.2K (Tab. 9).

GPT-3.5-turbo: HumanEval 57.3% zero-shot → 79.9% with AgentCoder; MBPP-ET 89.1% vs 63.0% for CodeCoT. Mean pass@1 across the four datasets is 84.1% (GPT-3.5) and 91.5% (GPT-4) against 75.3% and 86.8% for the best baselines, and it holds up on the harder enhanced sets (77.4/89.1) where base models collapse.

Ablation (Tab. 2): programmer alone 61.0/47.9 (HumanEval/MBPP) → +test designer 64.0/62.3 → programmer+executor 64.6/69.3 → full AgentCoder 79.9/89.9; both generated tests and real execution feedback are needed.

Test quality: designer-test accuracy 87.8/89.9 (GPT-3.5) and 89.6/91.4 (GPT-4), against MetaGPT (GPT-4) 79.3/84.4, CodeCoT 67.1/79.0, and plain GPT-3.5 47.0/57.2; line coverage 91.7/92.3 (GPT-4) vs MetaGPT 81.7/80.5 and CodeCoT 77.2/82.9.

Iterations 1→5 (GPT-3.5) raise pass@1 74.4→79.9 (HumanEval), 84.1→89.9 (MBPP), 80.3→89.1 (MBPP-ET); one agent doing both jobs is worse than two (test accuracy 61.0/51.8 vs 87.8/89.9, pass@1 71.3/79.4 vs 79.9/89.9).
advantages: Isolates why multi-agent code generation works: the win comes from a *non-oracle-biased test designer* plus a *real execution gate*, not from adding more agents — the executor is a plain Python script, so only two LLM calls are in the loop.

Cheapest of the measured multi-agent frameworks and the most accurate: 56.9K/66.3K tokens vs 138.2K+ for MetaGPT/ChatDev/AgentVerse, i.e. the paper's efficiency claim is bought by removing coordination chatter rather than by skimping on testing.

Ablations separate the contributions cleanly (Tab. 2, Tab. 6–8): a single agent asked to write code then tests loses ~27 points of test accuracy, quantifying the self-confirmation bias in code-then-test prompting.

Robustness under stricter tests: near-flat performance on HumanEval-ET/MBPP-ET is direct evidence the generated code is actually correct rather than tuned to the base datasets' two-or-three weak tests.
limitations: The paper has no limitations or broader-impact section: §5 says they are discussed in the Appendix, but Appendix A.1–A.6 contains only output-format setup, overhead, and case studies.
Scope is single-function generation on HumanEval/MBPP with ground-truth oracles; nothing is repository-scale, and no weights change, so every gain is in-context and evaporates at the end of the task.
The loop stops on 'all tests pass' or a fixed budget of 5 iterations: wrong designer oracles stall or misdirect the repair, and there is no mechanism to detect or discard a bad test.

Cost accounting counts response tokens only (no coordination/latency analysis of the failed iterations), and the abstract pairs the SOTA pass@1 (90.2/78.9, Self-Collaboration) with MetaGPT's token counts (138.2K/206.5K), misattributing the baseline comparison.
2312.13010.fits: Stage 7 'Iterative Repair & Training': the test-time repair loop Self-Debug (2304.05128) runs single-agent, here split into roles against an executed test oracle. It isolates the ingredients — generated tests, real execution, agent division — that SWE-Gym (2412.21139) later trains into weights and DGM/ASI (2505.22954, 2504.15228) turn on the agent's own code.
2312.13010.reading: §3 for the three agents (3.1 programmer CoT, 3.2 the test-designer prompt, 3.3 the executor script); §4.3–4.7 for the ablations (Tables 2–9). Appendix A.1–A.3 has the verbatim prompts and the ```py``` output-format contract.

2601.14525.tldr: Execution-Grounded AI Research: build an automated executor to implement ideas and launch parallel GPU experiments, then let the LLM learn from execution feedback.
2601.14525.method: Builds an automated executor that implements research ideas and launches large-scale parallel GPU experiments, then converts two real problems (LLM pre-training and LLM evaluation) into execution-grounded RL so the LLM learns from real execution.
results: Shows automated execution is feasible and that LLMs can learn from execution feedback on real research problems.

2601.14525.reading: Read the executor design and the two converted problems (§3–4).

2608.17906.method: Two stages: Idea Generation continuously integrates emerging research signals with accumulated domain knowledge to identify hypotheses; Idea Execution reliably establishes them through experimentation.

2607.28568.method: OpenMLE: open full-stack for RSI in MLE — verifiable task environments (Gym), operator learning (RL), long-horizon search (Evo) — on which a 35B model (Frontis-MA1) is post-trained as a meta-evolution agent.
