2603.01712.tldr: FT-Dojo is the first interactive benchmark for end-to-end LLM fine-tuning agents — 13 tasks across 5 domains with a shared raw-data pool, Docker sandbox and held-out evaluator; FT-Agent, a planning/fail-fast/feedback framework, wins 10 of 13 tasks.
2603.01712.method: FT-Dojo formalizes fine-tuning as argmax over data strategy θd and training hyperparameters θt, given structured feedback f(t). Each task supplies a natural-language objective plus an evaluation script; agents work inside a GPU-limited Docker sandbox against three interfaces — a Meta API (task spec, data descriptions, API docs), a shared raw-Data Repository (not per-task splits, so source selection is itself an optimization target), and an Evaluator built on OpenCompass returning aggregate metrics, per-instance predictions with correctness labels, and training loss curves. Validation and test splits are non-overlapping, each min(100, ⌊n/2⌋); training is capped at 2,000 self-constructed samples via SFT or LoRA on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct within a 12-hour single-B200 budget. FT-Agent adds structured iteration planning (compact data-strategy + training-config + rationale plans instead of verbose logs), three-stage fail-fast validation (schema/syntax, mini-run format check, runtime sanity), and multi-level feedback diagnosis that promotes a new best configuration when Fτ improves.
results: Best on 10 of 13 tasks (mean±std over 3 runs). AIME 2025: 0.00 → 11.11±3.82 accuracy, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, constrained Manual SFT and tool-augmented OpenHands all stay at 0.00 — the agent diagnosed missing reasoning supervision and synthesized CoT from a pool where 82% of samples lack solutions

Strongest where code or structural constraints are strict: Table QA Visualization Pass@1 29.33±6.11 vs OpenHands 24.00; Chemistry Molecule Editing 54.44±2.94 vs OpenHands 40.00. The losses are reported honestly — OpenHands wins both Reaction metrics (FTS 35.59 vs 30.92, Acc 60.00 vs 35.33) and Manual SFT wins Financial QA (71.68 vs 67.20)

Fail-fast validation converts budget into iterations: 6.0 vs 2.75 effective iterations inside the same 12h (2.2×; Table QA FC 7 vs 2), avg loops 8.77 vs 3.69, improvement rate 24.37% vs 17.31%, for $5.73 vs $3.92 of iterative spend

Five-task controlled comparison (same data repo, Docker env, LlamaFactory/OpenCompass wrappers, 12h): FT-Agent+GPT-5.2 averages 42.83, above Claude Code Sonnet-4.6-thinking (39.86), LLM-assisted Manual SFT (37.11), Codex GPT-5.2 (36.06) and OpenHands GPT-5.2 (34.55); swapping the planner to DeepSeek-V3.2 (35.83), GPT-4o (36.65) or Qwen3.5-397B (31.97) keeps it in range

Case-study duality: on Mol Edit the agent recovers from a 2% vocabulary-corruption collapse to 56% accuracy via format fixes and RDKit SMILES validation, but on PI4PC it shotguns generic fixes (NEFTune −11pp, collapse to 8%) and returns to the 34% baseline after 8 loops; on Visualization a locally-sane filter chain cut ~1,800 samples to 27 (98.5%) and dropped Pass@1 20% → 4%
advantages: First interactive, protocol-standardized environment for end-to-end fine-tuning: rather than per-task static datasets, it makes data curation and training configuration joint optimization targets under one fixed 2,000-sample budget, with a two-phase validation/test protocol that keeps the test set inaccessible during optimization

Unusually clean factorization — base model, raw data repository, Docker sandbox, training/eval wrappers, GPU, splits and wall clock are held fixed so only the agent framework varies — plus honest negative controls: doubling OpenHands to 24h on AIME changes nothing (best checkpoint lands in the first 6 hours), and scaling data 2k → 5k can hurt under a fixed budget because processing squeezes iteration time

Documents emergent autonomous cross-domain data transfer: for Numerical Reasoning the agent mixed in 10% out-of-domain DeepScaleR (AIME/AMC math) for 32.00 → 46.00 accuracy; for Mol Opt it built a 70/25/5 composite of mol_opt/mol_edit/mol_und for SR 23.33 → 36.67 with valid-SMILES 68.67 → 91.67 — and it stays selective, using only in-domain data on Reaction, Mol Edit and Mol Und

No black box: the paper's conflict-of-interest disclosure names the Microsoft authors behind FT-Agent, and the harness is released at github.com/microsoft/rd-agent with pluggable task-objective and evaluation-script modules, so new fine-tuning tasks need no core infrastructure changes
limitations: A benchmark, not a method, and the authors say so: the constituent datasets are pre-existing held-out evaluators (PANORAMA, ChemCoTBench, FinanceIQ, TableBench, AIME 2025), only the protocol is new; 13 tasks in 5 domains with pools from 4,497 to 136,211 raw samples is still narrow coverage

Causal diagnosis is the headline deficit: on PI4PC the agent describes symptoms with hedging language ('likely', 'appears') and applies generic ML techniques without asking why the task overfits, never operationalizing the train–eval mismatch it correctly named in Loop 2; net gain was zero

Planning myopia: the agent optimizes each pipeline step locally without modeling cumulative state changes, which is exactly how the Visualization dataset collapsed 98.5%; a 3-stage validation gate cannot catch joint effects that only appear after composition

Statistics are uneven by necessity: 3 seeds for FT-Agent only (full coverage would cost 1,500+ GPU-hours, so baselines are single controlled runs) and chemistry reaction similarity is volatile (30.92±11.22), which the paper flags as large variance; one author group also built both the benchmark and the winning agent
2603.01712.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D) — the 'fine-tuning as an agent task' environment, one level above MLE-Bench/DSBench and below MLEvolve. Pairs with MLE-Dojo and MLE-Bench as the fixed-data vs open-data contrast, and with the autoresearch/rd-agent harnesses: FT-Agent is the feedback-and-reward-signal half, hyperagents the self-modification half.
2603.01712.reading: Read §2.1–2.4 for the task formulation, two-phase validation/test protocol and 2k budget; §3 for the three FT-Agent mechanisms; §4.2–4.5 with Tables 2–4; and Appendix D for the Mol Edit recovery vs PI4PC shotgun-debugging traces.

2606.06473.tldr: An LLM multi-agent framework that evolves end-to-end ML algorithms, reaching 65.3% average medal rate on MLE-Bench in a 12-hour budget — best among compared agents at half the standard 24h runtime — and the best result on 11 of 15 AlphaEvolve math-optimization tasks.
2606.06473.method: Three coupled mechanisms per task (500 steps, 12h). A branch is a root-to-leaf trajectory of candidate solutions (3 initial drafts, max 5 branches plus 2 fusion). (1) Progressive MCGS: primary edges carry UCT selection and backpropagation; reference edges — never backpropagated — point from other branches' top nodes, so cross-branch transfer conditions generation on retrieved solutions, not scalar rewards. A soft switch w(t) decays 1.0→0.2, blending UCT exploration into Elite-Guided picks from the global top-3 by inverse rank; two-level stagnation detection (τ_branch=3, τ_global=6) triggers intra-branch evolution, cross-branch fusion, or multi-branch aggregation at the root. (2) Retrospective Memory: curated cold-start knowledge base plus a dynamic global store of per-node records (plan, outcome, metric, analysis), retrieved by BM25+FAISS fused via RRF at planning/debugging stages — records persist across the run, replacing memoryless scalar-only search. (3) Planner-coder decoupling: planner decides what/why at module level; coder implements via Base/Stepwise/Diff modes chosen by search state.
results: MLE-Bench (75 tasks, 12h budget, 3 seeds): 65.3% average medal rate, 34.7% gold, 100% valid submissions, 76.0% above-median — vs. best 24h baselines MARS+ 62.7% medal / 33.8% gold and AIBuildAI 63.1% / 25.8%; by complexity 80.3% low, 64.0% medium, 46.7% high.

AlphaEvolve's 15 math-optimization tasks: best result on 11 of 15 vs. AlphaEvolve, AlphaEvolve-v2, SimpleTES, TTT-Discover, and OpenEvolve (e.g., sums-differences problem 1: 1.1901774219 vs. AlphaEvolve's 1.1479889651; circle packing in a rectangle: 2.3658323759 vs. 2.3658321334).

Component ablation on MLE-Bench Lite (22 tasks): medal 81.82% full → 68.18% w/o Progressive MCGS, 68.18% w/o Retrospective Memory (the paper's cited 13.64% drop), 72.73% w/o adaptive code generation; beat ratio 88.39% vs. 79.91/81.90/84.14.

Search dynamics: effective active branches exp(H(π)) falls 4.8 → 2.8 over the run (vanilla MCTS flat at ~4.3); on representative tasks beat ratio reaches 98.2% vs. ~70% for vanilla MCTS, which plateaus early.

Mechanism-level ablation (9-task subset): removing intra-branch evolution drops medal 66.67% → 33.33% (largest single factor); removing the knowledge base or the global memory each drops it to 44.44%.
advantages: State-of-the-art MLE-Bench result at half the standard 24-hour budget (65.3% vs. MARS+ 62.7% and AIBuildAI 63.1%, both at 24h) with 100% valid submissions — an efficiency claim, not just a score claim.

Cross-domain check most MLE agents skip: unchanged, it beats specialized algorithm-discovery systems (AlphaEvolve, AlphaEvolve-v2, OpenEvolve) on 11/15 math tasks, evidence the search machinery generalizes past Kaggle.

Reference edges are a clean way to get cross-branch information flow without corrupting credit assignment — backpropagation stays strictly on primary edges — and every mechanism ablates positively, with intra-branch evolution isolated as the critical one.

Memory accumulates without extra reflection LLM calls: records are logged by a Result Parse Agent and retrieved by BM25+FAISS/RRF, unlike MARS/ROME-style reflection memory, and the two memory halves (static KB vs. dynamic store) are separately ablatable.
limitations: Expensive per task: up to 500 expansion steps over 12h on 21 vCPUs / 234GB RAM, an H200 GPU, and a frontier backbone (Gemini-3.1-Pro-preview); baseline numbers are taken from leaderboards or papers, so comparisons confound framework with different backbone LLMs and budgets.

The edge shrinks with difficulty: 46.7% medal on high-complexity tasks only ties AIBuildAI's 46.7% (at 24h), vs. 80.3% on low-complexity — most of the gain over MARS+ comes from medium tasks (64.0% vs. 60.5%).

The cold-start knowledge base is manually curated per task type from repositories and competition platforms, so part of performance is static human prior rather than self-evolved; the dynamic memory is task-scoped, not accumulated across tasks (ML-Master 2.0's cross-task caching is the contrast).
Ablation statistics are thin: 22 tasks (Lite) for component removal, 9 tasks for mechanism analysis, and some headline cells carry ±0.0 SEM over 3 seeds (gold rate, valid rate, high-complexity).
2606.06473.fits: Stage-8 descendant of AutoML-Zero/AlphaEvolve for whole-ML-algorithm discovery (the repo positions it as AutoMLGen's successor): it keeps the propose-execute-evaluate loop but adds machinery that makes long-horizon search persistent — graph reference edges for cross-branch reuse, an entropy schedule shifting exploration toward exploitation, run-length experience memory, and planner/coder decoupling.
2606.06473.reading: §3.2 (Progressive MCGS, Eqs. 3–7, four expansion types), §3.3 (memory + RRF retrieval), §4.2 Tables 1–2, §4.3 Table 3 plus Appendix E Table 5, §4.4 Fig 3 (entropy dynamics).

2601.10657.tldr: PACEvolve diagnoses three failure modes of LLM-driven evolutionary search — context pollution, mode collapse, weak collaboration — and fixes them with hierarchical idea memory, momentum-triggered backtracking, and self-adaptive cross-island crossover, reaching state-of-the-art on symbolic regression, KernelBench, and Modded NanoGPT.
2601.10657.method: From 200+ 1000-step evolution runs the authors find append-only history contexts saturate with failed trials (context pollution), agents anchor to locally similar hypotheses (mode collapse), and static periodic crossover wastes parallel compute (weak collaboration). PACEvolve evolves candidate solutions (equations, GPU kernels, training code) via three mechanisms. HCM decouples idea generation from selection over a persistent idea pool (caps: 5 ideas, 20 hypotheses each): an LLM classifier merges conceptually duplicate ideas, caps trigger summarization and LLM pruning, and a permanent failure log preserves consistency by blocking rediscovery of dead ends. MBB computes scale-invariant Relative Progress R_t (fraction of remaining gap G_t = s_t − r closed), smoothed into momentum m_t by EWMA (β=0.85); when m_t < 0.001 the trajectory reverts to an ancestor state drawn from a power-law (α=1.5), resetting context. CE then samples backtrack vs. crossover from other islands with probability proportional to absolute-progress-based weights.
results: LLM-SR nonlinear-oscillator symbolic regression (Log10 NMSE, 10 runs × 1000 iterations, Gemini 2.5 Pro): PACEvolve-Multi best −8.24 / P75 −7.64 / mean −6.11 vs ShinkaEvolve −6.35 / −5.92 / −5.35, OpenEvolve −7.11 / −5.79 / −5.40, and non-LLM uDSR best −4.06; Multi finds 3 solutions below log10 NMSE −8.

KernelBench (16 kernels, 1000 iterations each, A100 40GB): beats the best KernelBench-leaderboard kernel on all 16, beats ShinkaEvolve on all 16 (PACE-Multi ≥ Single on 13/16, i.e. 81.25%), matches-or-beats OpenEvolve on 15/16 and CodeEvolve/ShinkaEvolve on 14/16; up to 17.38× over PyTorch (LayerNorm, 10.1ms → 0.581ms), though it loses to PyTorch on MLP/MatMul.

Modded NanoGPT (8×H100, Gemini 3 Pro): cuts time to val loss 3.28 on FineWeb from the heavily optimized v40 baseline 142.8s → 140.2s via data sharding/preloading, U-shaped skip-connection init (0.8→0.4→0.8), hyperparameter tuning, and dynamic context scheduling — on a benchmark already optimized from ~2700s (v1) to 142s.

Ablation (10 runs each): HCM lifts mean/best but worst runs still stall (a locally-optimal idea is never erased); adding MBB eliminates stalled trajectories yet slightly hurts best runs (exploration tax); adding CE recovers top-run performance while keeping the floor — full stack needed.
advantages: Real diagnosis, not anecdote: 200+ 1000-step runs show trajectories that fail to find low-NMSE solutions in the first few iterations rarely recover, with large variance across independent runs (Fig. 2) — grounding context pollution and mode collapse in measured search dynamics.
Each failure mode gets a matched, ablation-isolated fix: HCM's bi-level pruning cleans context, and MBB's progress-aware trigger removes the worst-run tail that context erasure alone cannot (§4.3).

The scale-invariant Relative Progress metric lets one stagnation trigger work across tasks without task-specific thresholds, unlike fixed-schedule resets in ShinkaEvolve/FunSearch-style loops that ignore search state.
Same scaffold achieves SOTA across three distinct domains — scientific equation discovery, GPU kernel optimization, and full-stack distributed training engineering — suggesting the recipe transfers.
limitations: By the paper's own ablation, backtracking 'slightly affected the best-performing processes' (exploration taxes exploitation), and CE only helps 'provided that at least one island discovers a promising direction' — joint all-island stagnation remains a risk.

No explicit limitations section; the authors flag KernelBench/Modded-NanoGPT world knowledge as 'questionable' (Table 5) since optimization strategies likely sit in LLM pretraining corpora, so gains may partly reflect retrieval rather than search.

Tasks need smooth rewards and cheap evaluation per the paper's own criteria; Modded NanoGPT needs 8 H100s and its gain is incremental (142.8s → 140.2s, conceded as 'this improvement looks incremental').

Mechanism assumes a known metric lower bound r and tuned constants (β=0.85, ε_rel=0.001, caps 5/20, power-law exponent 1.5); a sweep (Fig. 5) reports robustness but values are still benchmark-derived.
2601.10657.fits: Stage-9 prerequisite: open-ended evolution stalls without memory governance — long-horizon search needs structured, pruned idea memory plus a progress signal that decides when to abandon a line of work. Its diagnosis-first methodology (measure failure modes across 200+ runs, then derive the scaffold) pairs naturally with PACE-style diagnosis in this catalog.
2601.10657.reading: Read §2 (failure-mode study), §3.1–3.3 (HCM, MBB, CE with the Relative Progress equations), §4.3 (ablation), and Appendix A (case-study insights); Appendix B has pseudocode and hyperparameters (β=0.85, ε=0.001, caps 5/20).

openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.tldr: Higher-order evolution: evolve the mutation rate, recursively the meta-mutation rate, up to a self-referential top-level parameter that modifies itself.
openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.method: Evolves higher-order parameters (mutation rate → meta-mutation rate → … up to a self-referential top-level parameter that modifies itself), showing this improves robustness in Population-Based Training and Unsupervised Environment Design.
results: Self-referential mutation improves robustness to initial hyperparameters and enables complex adaptation in competitive multi-agent settings.
limitations: Small-scale domains (PBT/UED); self-referential levels are still bounded in practice.
openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.fits: The evolutionary-computation counterpart to the Gödel Agent — the meta-parameters of evolution are themselves evolved, one step toward self-referential search.
openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.reading: Read the higher-order/self-referential mutation definitions (§2–3) and the PBT/UED results.

1901.01753.tldr: POET: co-evolve environments and their solutions, transferring solutions between niches — an endless self-generated curriculum of stepping stones.
1901.01753.method: Co-evolves a population of environments and their specialized solutions; solutions transfer between niches, and the system continually generates more complex/diverse environments.
results: Finds solutions to problems it never directly targeted (stepping-stone transfer), including a hard-to-discover bipedal walker via indirect transfer.
limitations: Simple 2D-locomotion domains; the open-ended loop is hard to stabilize and scale.
1901.01753.fits: The canonical 'generate your own problems' system — POWERPLAY made evolutionary and open-ended; the lineage behind UED and modern self-generated curricula.
1901.01753.reading: Read the co-evolution + transfer mechanism (§3) and the stepping-stone result (§4).

agent-zero.what: A general-purpose agent framework that gives the agent a full Linux computer — a Dockerized desktop, annotated browser, document cowork, skills/plugins, and a bridge back to your host.
architecture: Dockerized Linux desktop + browser with DOM annotation for real computer/GUI control.
Projects, skills, and plugins as persistent capabilities the agent composes.
Host bridge lets the agent act on and coordinate with the user's own machine.
agent-zero.run: Docker-based: `docker compose up` (see the Quick Start in the README) launches the desktop + browser; add your LLM API key.
agent-zero.note: An 'extensible substrate' — the harness *is* a whole computer. Study it for how an OS-level workspace generalizes far beyond a chat loop.

deepseek-harness.what: DeepSeek's open-source agent harness (`dsh`): a TypeScript monorepo where every component — model adapters, tool registry, session log, the agent loop itself — is a Cordis plugin, composed at boot into replaceable profiles (web, headless, sdk, sdk-minimal, acp). MIT, developer preview.
architecture: Everything-is-a-plugin via Cordis (its design is formalized in arXiv 2608.25512, 'A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability'): plugins contribute services, typed events, and reversible effects to one shared context; there is no privileged core — the model adapter, tool registry, session log, and agent loop (`ctx.agentLoop`) are all rows replaceable from config, and registrations unwind when their plugin unloads.

Boot composition is ordered layers: each profile stacks bundles, then the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, then the home-level one, then `--patch` overlays; a patch targets a config row by id and replaces its whole config, and `dsh --profile web --dump-config` prints the exact tree your machine boots.

The session log is the source of truth: an append-only `SessionEvent` log under a runtime invariant that anything reaching a model request must be reconstructable from it ('model-visible means logged'); `deriveMessages()` projects model history, and storage is versioned `session.vN.jsonl[.zstd]` generations with one-step migration chains — fork, resume, transcripts, and telemetry all derive from it.

Tools register with `defineTool` (typed params, validated calls, allow/deny/ask policy) and their schemas join prompt assembly automatically; native function-calling or PTC mode, where a `run_code` program calls registry tools through nested sub-dispatches — each logged for reconstruction, only the outer curated result entering model history; `maxParallelToolCalls` defaults to 10. Capability seams (Service Definition + Provider + Consumer) swap fs and subprocess together, so one provider change moves Bash, PTY, and LSP to a remote sandbox with no forks.
advantages: The interception surface a self-modification experiment needs is first-class, not monkey-patched: `agent/pre-step` rewrites or rejects claimed input, `agent/request` reroutes model calls, `tools/pre-execute|execute|post-execute` guard tool runs, and `agent/turn-stopping` stops a turn — every extension point is a typed event with a documented producer/consumer map.

Harness-as-data: because the running agent is a patchable config tree with YAML-driven HMR, you can inspect, re-compose, or shrink the harness itself (`sdk-minimal` is a complete explicit SDK tree that omits `dsh-base`) through the same mechanism plugins use to extend it.

A coordination substrate for multi-agent RSI: experimental Agent Teams on `ctx.agentTeams` (durable roster, task board, mailbox over continuable subagents), forkable sessions at turn boundaries, and swappable subagent providers — including a one-shot provider that delegates a task to a fresh, unattended Claude Code session in the parent workspace.
deepseek-harness.run: `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` — Web UI at http://127.0.0.1:3080 (needs Node.js; `--no-open` skips the browser). From source: `git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness && cd deepseek-harness && pnpm install && pnpm run build && pnpm dsh web`. Other profiles: `dsh --profile headless|sdk|sdk-minimal|acp`.
deepseek-harness.note: Read docs/architecture.md first — its turn-flow event map and 'where new behavior goes' table are the real spec. Then trace one turn's events end-to-end and study the patch mechanism as the harness self-modification seam. Mind SAFETY.md: unaudited preview that executes model-generated code and third-party plugins.

openclaw.what: Open-source, self-hosted personal AI assistant (TypeScript on Node, MIT, stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation 501(c)(3)): an always-on local Gateway drives agent sessions from your existing chats — WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, iMessage, 20+ more — with state, memory, and credentials on your own hardware.
architecture: The Gateway is the whole architecture: one local, always-on control plane for sessions, tools, events, and channel connections; CLI, TUI, and Control UI attach to it, and the identical Gateway runs a laptop assistant or a shared team deployment — configuration is the only difference. Channels bring it to 20+ chat networks; companion apps and nodes add voice, Canvas, camera, screen, and device-local actions.

Trusted gateway / untrusted execution with policy as code: denial is structural, not a request the model is asked to honor — src/gateway/agent-turn/agent-admission-controller.ts admits runs through session-work admission leases and dedupe reservations that fail closed (aborted/timeout/superseded outcomes, fail on deleted or archived sessions). Sandboxing (docker or OpenShell kernel-level backends, agents.defaults.sandbox.mode: "all"), exec approvals, DM sender pairing, and `openclaw security audit --deep` are explicit configuration, off by default.

Vendor harnesses are first-class swappable plugins, not API endpoints: the Codex plugin drives Codex's own app-server loop, the Anthropic plugin drives the installed Claude Code executable over its structured stdio protocol, while OpenClaw keeps ownership of channels, sessions, policy, and state. The core stays deliberately small — channels, memory, and harnesses are all plugins behind capability-registration points enforced by CI import guards, with a public plugin SDK of about 150 entrypoints under shrink-only surface budgets.

Extensibility and state have their own mechanisms: skills follow the AgentSkills spec and ship through the ClawHub registry (moderation, VirusTotal/ClawScan/static-analysis scan status, `openclaw skills verify`); memory carries provenance with explicit deletion (`openclaw memory forget`); state is schema-versioned with guarded migrations owned by `openclaw doctor`; interoperates over MCP (client and server), A2A 1.0, and ACP. Default telemetry is a single daily version check; `update.checkOnStart: false` disables it.
advantages: The clearest production answer to what an always-on, credential-holding personal agent must fix before self-improvement is safe: secrets via handles with egress substitution so the model never sees them, versioned state with guarded upgrades, purgeable memory with reingestion barriers, recorded provenance and audit — each a named, code-level mechanism, formalized as seven testable harness properties in Why OpenClaw.

Harness portability made concrete: one operator-owned loop that can drive Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, or local models as plugins keeps harness, policy, and state as inspectable, separately-replaceable layers — the exact factoring that harness-evolving RSI work tends to blur.

A field-tested threat model for long-lived autonomous agents: ~390k stars with chat-network ingress and real credentials, 647 published security advisories (as of 2026-08-27), public trust model, and an academic security case study of the architecture (arXiv 2603.12644); NVIDIA's NemoClaw distribution hardens it with OpenShell sandboxing.
openclaw.run:
curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash   # macOS / Linux / WSL2 (Windows PowerShell: iwr -useb https://openclaw.ai/install.ps1 | iex)
npm install -g openclaw@latest --allow-scripts=openclaw   # if you manage Node yourself (24.16+ or 26.1+; 26 recommended)
openclaw onboard --install-daemon   # after install; then: openclaw gateway status && openclaw dashboard
openclaw.note: Read the seven testable harness properties in Why OpenClaw, then check them against code: agent-admission-controller.ts (fail-closed admission), the plugin capability-registration points, ClawHub skill verification. Policy-in-code vs policy-in-prompt is where it becomes functions — what a self-modifying agent may touch, what persists, who approves.

pi.what: Minimal, extensible terminal coding agent and harness (pi.dev) whose centerpiece is a self-extensible agent: it writes its own TypeScript extensions, skills, and prompt templates, layered on a stateful agent runtime and a unified multi-provider LLM API.
architecture: Layered monorepo: `pi-coding-agent` (interactive CLI, bin `pi`) builds on `pi-agent-core` (stateful `Agent` with tool execution and event streaming), which builds on `pi-ai` (unified multi-provider LLM API: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, …); sibling packages add `pi-tui`, `pi-durable`, `pi-telemetry`, and `chord`.

Self-extension = in-process TypeScript extensions: a default factory receives `ExtensionAPI` and registers tools (`pi.registerTool()`), commands, providers, and event handlers; loaded via `jiti` (no compile step) from `~/.pi/agent/extensions/` or project dirs, or ad hoc with `pi --extension ./hello.ts`. The README's pitch: 'Ask Pi to create the prompt templates, skills, extensions, and themes you need.'

The agent mutates its own tool set at runtime: register every tool, keep optional ones inactive, and a loader tool calls `pi.setActiveTools()`; `examples/extensions/dynamic-tools.ts` registers brand-new tools mid-session. Pi logs the initial prompt/tool set in the transcript's first system message and appends each tool/prompt change before the next model request.

Sessions are JSONL trees — every entry has an ID and parent, branches fork from any entry, compaction inserts summary entries — and all five interfaces (interactive, print, JSON, RPC, TypeScript SDK) share the same agent/session mechanisms. Skills inject instructions on demand.
advantages: The extension API is ordinary in-process TypeScript the agent itself can author and reload (`ctx.reload()`), so self-extension is a first-class loop — a concrete substrate for studying agents that grow their own tool sets rather than a metaphor.
Each layer is independently reusable: build a custom agent on `pi-agent-core` + `pi-ai` (a dozen lines to stream a tool-calling agent) without adopting the coding agent.
Branch-tree sessions with compaction and forking yield durable, inspectable transcripts; the project actively curates real OSS agent sessions as datasets (badlogicgames/pi-mono on Hugging Face).
pi.run:
npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent  # Node >= 22.19; or: curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh
cd /path/to/project && pi   # then /login to attach a provider
pi.note: Read packages/coding-agent/docs/extensions.md and how-pi-works.md, then examples/extensions/dynamic-tools.ts: new tools registered mid-session, active set switched via pi.setActiveTools(). Deliberately ships no built-in permission system — docs/containerization.md covers micro-VM/Docker sandboxing.

hermes-agent.what: Nous Research's MIT-licensed general-purpose Python agent — AIAgent core behind a CLI, messaging gateway, and Electron desktop shell — whose headline is a closed self-improvement loop: the agent writes its own skills, curates its bounded memory, searches its past sessions, and prunes both in the background.
architecture: AIAgent core (run_agent.py facade; loop in agent/conversation_loop.py + turn_*.py): 3 API modes (chat completions, codex responses, anthropic), 70+ tools across 28 toolsets, `delegate_task` subagents, and 7 terminal backends (local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox), fronted by CLI/TUI, an Electron shell (apps/desktop), and one gateway process bridging Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp/Signal/email; session storage is SQLite + FTS5.

Procedural memory: agentskills.io-compatible SKILL.md files in ~/.hermes/skills loaded by progressive disclosure (a ≤60-char description indexed every session — past char 60 it is silently cut and never routes; `skill_view` loads bodies on demand). The agent authors its own via `skill_manage` (create/patch/delete/write_file) under HARDLINE authoring standards, with an advisory linter (incident-log-shape, references-sprawl >60 files, oversized-body ~24k chars); `/learn` distills any source into a skill or a lean-index knowledge base (SKILL.md + per-chapter references/).

Episodic memory: MEMORY.md (2,200 chars ≈800 tokens) and USER.md (1,375 chars ≈500 tokens) injected as a frozen session-start snapshot (preserves prefix cache); the `memory` tool does add/replace/remove only — no read — and returns an error when full, forcing the agent to consolidate in-turn before retrying. `session_search` (FTS5, custom fts5_cjk extension) with LLM summarization recalls past sessions; Honcho supplies dialectic user modeling.

The learning loop is background machinery, not a training loop: after each turn a forked AIAgent (agent/background_review.py, auxiliary.background_review.enabled default true) replays the conversation snapshot asking 'should any skill/memory be saved or updated?' and writes straight to the stores — inheriting the parent's runtime and prompt-cache prefix, whitelist-gated tools, isolated session id — gated by nudge counters (memory.nudge_interval default 10; skills.creation_nudge_interval); plus the inactivity-triggered Curator (agent/curator.py): 7-day interval, 2h min idle, stale after 14 unused days, archived (never deleted) after 30, opt-in aux-model consolidation fork, before/after-hash ledger with rollback.
advantages: A production-grade instance of the experience→procedural-memory loop (Voyager-style skill libraries, but for a deployed agent): usage telemetry (~/.hermes/skills/.usage.json, `created_by: agent` markers), a linter, lifecycle states (active→stale→archived), and approval gates specify the parts research scaffolds leave implicit.

Every self-write is observable and reversible: skill mutations append before/after hashes to .curator_ledger.jsonl (`hermes curator rollback`), the curator only ever archives, and skills.write_approval / memory.write_approval stage agent writes for human review — a working model of gated self-modification.

Ships the data flywheel: batch trajectory generation writes ShareGPT-format JSONL (trajectory_samples.jsonl vs failed_trajectories.jsonl by completion, <REASONING_SCRATCHPAD> normalized to <think>) explicitly for 'training the next generation of tool-calling models'.
hermes-agent.run: curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash   (Windows: iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1)); then `source ~/.bashrc && hermes`; `hermes model` picks a provider (OpenRouter/OpenAI/Nous Portal/own endpoint), `hermes gateway` starts the messaging bridge. Dev: `uv pip install -e ".[all,dev]"` in the installer's checkout at ~/.hermes/hermes-agent.
hermes-agent.note: Read agent/background_review.py (the post-turn 'should this be saved?' fork and its persistence-isolation guards) and agent/curator.py (7d/2h/14d/30d lifecycle) against config_defaults.py. Contrast with DGM: Hermes improves its memory and procedures, never its own code — self-improvement as curation, not metaprogramming.

seal.what: SEAL (Self-Adapting LLMs) trains models via RL to generate *self-edits* — their own finetuning data and update directives — in response to new inputs.
architecture: RL loop where the model proposes edits (finetuning data + update directives) to itself.
Two domains: general-knowledge (absorb new facts) and few-shot (adapt to new tasks).
MIT CSAIL; code + data for both domains in the repo.
seal.run: Python; `git clone`, set up a conda/venv (README §Setup), then run the domain scripts.
seal.note: A model-level self-improvement substrate: the model writes the *data and update instructions* for its own adaptation — a concrete bridge between weight-space and data-space RSI.

letta-code.what: A stateful agent harness where agents have memory, identity, and experience — and can rewrite their own memory, skills, prompts, and the harness itself via 'mods'.
architecture: Stateful agents with persistent memory/identity/experience over long horizons.
Self-modification: agents rewrite their own memory, skills, prompts, and harness (mods).
Surfaces: CLI, desktop app, browser (chat.letta.com), and messaging channels.
letta-code.run: `npx @letta-ai/letta-code` for the CLI; desktop app available for macOS/Windows/Linux.
letta-code.note: One of the most direct 'harness that modifies itself' products — study the mods mechanism for how self-modification is scoped safely.

memento-skills.what: Memento-S: a skill-centric agent runtime where skills are the unit of capability — retrieved, executed, authored, and repaired in deployment. Agents design agents via guarded skill evolution; the accompanying study shows deployment-time skill learning (frozen weights) improving GAIA and HLE over reflective rounds.
architecture: Skills as SKILL.md + scripts directories under builtin/skills/ (filesystem, web-search, skill-creator, uv-pip-install), loaded by core/skill/loader/, modeled in core/skill/schema.py (pydantic Skill with JSON-schema parameters, default a single natural-language `request`), persisted through db/file/vector backends in core/skill/store/.

4-phase pipeline in core/memento_s/phases/: intent.py → planning.py (the *Architect* emits a TaskPlan of PlanSteps at single-skill granularity with input_from dataflow) → execution/ (multi-step ReAct loop split into runner, tool_handler, step_boundary, guarded by hooks/ loop_detector, sandbox_audit, policy/tool_gate) → reflection.py (the *Supervisor* decides continue/replan/finalize/ASK_USER) and finalize.py.

Agents design agents in two places: core/skill/evolution/engine.py — transactional write phase that attributes a failed trace to one skill (confidence-scored), LLM-rewrites files in an isolated copy, gates it on static/unit/synthetic-judge tests, then deploys atomically or rolls back — plus builtin/skills/skill-creator/ (analyzer/comparator/grader sub-agents, run_eval.py, package_skill.py) for authoring new skills from scratch.

Routing over the library via core/skill/retrieval/ (local_recall BM25+vector, qwen_recall.py Qwen3/Memento-Qwen embeddings, remote_recall, multi_recall fusion) feeding core/memento_s/skill_dispatch/ (hallucination_guard, post_install); unified tools/registry.py wraps tools/atomics/ + MCP; surfaces: memento agent CLI, Flet memento-gui desktop app, core/skill/market.py cloud catalogue with downloader/github.py, and daemon/dream/ consolidator that mines sessions into skill candidates.
advantages: The only catalog entry where self-modification is transactional: attribution → isolated file-level rewrite → static/unit/synthetic gates → atomic deploy or rollback, with audit history — a worked answer to 'how does an agent safely edit its own capabilities', vs. code-as-skill systems (Voyager, AgentFactory) that write skills without candidate gating.

Deployment-time learning with frozen parameters (θ frozen, behaviour stored in external skill memory M): the GAIA/HLE round-over-round gains make it a concrete substrate for studying skill-memory growth curves instead of fine-tuning.

Ships as a real product, not a benchmark script — CLI, Windows/macOS desktop app, IM gateways, Skill Market — so you can test whether learned skills persist and transfer across live sessions, and compare its SKILL.md packaging (Anthropic-compatible, per THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES) against OpenClaw's deployment-first take.
memento-skills.run: git clone https://github.com/Memento-Teams/Memento-Skills.git && cd Memento-Skills && python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -e . && memento doctor && memento agent  # configure ~/memento_s/config.json (llm profile + TAVILY_API_KEY); GUI: memento-gui; or desktop app from memento.run/release

Compare its transactional skill repair and SKILL.md format with Voyager/AgentFactory code-as-skill.

reef.what: First open-source infrastructure for continual self-improving agents: an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible serving layer that records interactions, matches feedback to receipts, trains weights (Slime/SGLang) or evolves harness text (Reefine), and publishes only evaluation-passing updates as versioned releases while serving continues.
architecture: Serve-Observe-Grow-Commit loop mapped to real modules (README table): reef/service/ takes OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible requests (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/messages) and records interactions; reef/storage/records.py stores AgentRecords; reef/train/processors/ match reported feedback to eligibility; reef/recipe/ + reef/train/ produce the update; reef/train/evaluation/ + reef/artifact/ gate and publish it.

Feedback is receipt-based: every response carries an x-reef-agent-record-id header; POST /reef/report attaches {score, feedback, references:[receipt]} validated against schemas in reef/core/reports/ (scored_rollout, teacher_context); the x-reef-scenario request header creates or selects the scenario whose recipe decides what evolves — requests never pick recipes.

Backends are pluggable: reef/train/slime_backend/ (Megatron LoRA adapters, Ray executors, weight_updaters) and tinker_backend/ train weights; reef/train/cordis_backend/ proposes harness Mutations; recipes (sao, tttd, gepa, meta_harness, openclawrl, skillclaw) live in the recipes/ cookbook, selected by dotted class reference and not shipped in the wheel.

Versioned delivery: reef/artifact/ keeps an immutable parent-linked release chain (fork, publish with expected_parent, staged commit_release, git+LFS) and rejected candidates never move the serving release; reef/train/evaluation/evaluators.py ships RegressionCheckMixin — select only while the metric stays within margin of the best so far, so serving holds last selected weights — and reef/surface/ delivers accepted artifacts to harness adapters (pi, claude, codex, opencode, terminus).
advantages: The only substrate here that learns under live traffic: serving and training share the deployment, updated weights sync in without a restart, and a rejected candidate leaves the current release serving — unlike offline search loops (RRSI) or batch RL frameworks, both of which stop the world to improve.

One receipt/report plumbing over two artifacts: model weights (SAO continual learning; TTT-Discover test-time training with measured TriMul, circle-packing and Erdos minimum-overlap results) or harness text (Reefine writes a change as a skill, rules entry, agent command, or pi extension and test-runs it under bwrap/pasta sandboxing) — weight-level and harness-level RSI in one deployment.

Non-regression is a first-class policy, not a convention: each candidate-evaluation plugin implements evaluate() and decide() in one contract, with best-checkpoint selection running online against the deployment's own traffic.
reef.run: Python 3.12+, git-lfs required for artifacts. `uv venv && source .venv/bin/activate && uv pip install reef-infra`, then a pure inference server: `uv run reef serve --inference.model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`. Harness evolution (no GPUs): `reef serve --recipe reefine --inference.upstream-url http://127.0.0.1:11434 --inference.upstream-model gemma4:26b`, then `reef-pi evolve "..."`. Weight training adds `uv pip install -e ".[slime]" && uv pip install --no-deps --group runtime`.
reef.note: Trace the core loop from reef/service/app.py through reef/artifact/release_chain.py; read train/evaluation/evaluators.py (RegressionCheckMixin is the online non-regression gate) and compare recipes/sao/ (weights) with reef/recipe/reefine/evolution.py (harness) — the same loop over two artifact types.

autoresearch.what: Karpathy's experiment: hand an AI agent a small but real LLM-training setup (a simplified single-GPU nanochat) and let it edit the training code autonomously overnight, keeping only the changes that lower validation bits-per-byte.
architecture: The harness is program.md, 'a super lightweight skill': the agent cuts a branch autoresearch/<tag>, then LOOP FOREVER — edit train.py, git commit, run `uv run train.py > run.log 2>&1`, extract results with `grep "^val_bpb:\|^peak_vram_mb:" run.log`, log an untracked results.tsv row (commit, val_bpb, memory_gb, keep/discard/crash, description), keep the commit if val_bpb dropped, otherwise git reset. Runs over 10 minutes are killed and reverted; crashes are logged as status 'crash' with val_bpb 0.000000. A NEVER STOP clause forbids pausing to ask the human — ~12 experiments/hour, ~100 per night.

Scope split over exactly three files: the agent may edit only train.py — 'everything is fair game' (architecture, optimizer, hyperparameters, batch size, model size; baseline is DEPTH 8 → 512-dim, Muon at lr 0.04 for matrices + Adam for embeddings 0.6 / unembedding 0.004 / scalars 0.5, total batch 2^19, 'SSSL' sliding-window attention, FA3 kernels). prepare.py is read-only, no new packages allowed.

The gate is evaluate_bpb in prepare.py ('DO NOT CHANGE — this is the fixed metric'): validation bits-per-byte on a pinned shard (shard_06542 of climbmix-400b-shuffle), ~21M eval tokens (EVAL_TOKENS = 40 × 524,288) at MAX_SEQ_LEN 2048 — sums per-token cross-entropy in nats over target byte lengths, special tokens excluded; vocab-size-independent so architecture changes compare fairly.

Fixed 300-second wall-clock training budget (first 10 compile/warmup steps excluded) keeps every experiment directly comparable and auto-tunes to your GPU; training fast-fails if loss is NaN or > 100. Soft constraints: VRAM shouldn't blow up, and a simplicity criterion — a ~0.001 val_bpb gain for 20 hacky lines is 'probably not worth it', while equal-or-better results from deleting code is a win.
Baseline printed by the stock config (example in program.md): val_bpb 0.997900, 953 steps, 499.6M tokens, 50.3M params, 44.0 GB peak VRAM, 39.8% MFU in 300.1s on an H100.
advantages: Time-boxed equal-budget comparisons: because every run costs exactly 5 minutes regardless of what changed, results stay comparable across radical architecture rewrites, and the search finds the best model for your specific hardware rather than a leaderboard config.

Cleanly separates what evolves from what judges: train.py (agent-editable), prepare.py (immutable evaluator), program.md (human-editable 'research org code') — so you can study or iterate on the improvement policy itself, not just the code it improves.
Fully auditable by construction: each experiment is a git commit on the run branch plus a results.tsv row, keeping diffs reviewable and the overnight history replayable.
autoresearch.run: Install uv (`curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`), then: `uv sync`; `uv run prepare.py` (one-time data + BPE tokenizer, ~2 min); `uv run train.py` (one ~5-min experiment). For autonomous mode, spin up Claude/Codex in the repo with all permissions disabled and prompt: 'Hi have a look at program.md and let's kick off a new experiment! let's do the setup first.'
autoresearch.note: Read program.md first — the loop, keep/discard rule, crash policy, and NEVER STOP clause are the entire harness; then evaluate_bpb in prepare.py, the gate the agent may not touch. Distinct from the AutoResearch paper (arXiv 2608.17906).

evolutionary-model-merge.what: Sakana AI's hub for the Evolutionary Model Merge series (Nature Machine Intelligence 2025): the released EvoLLM-JP / EvoVLM-JP merged checkpoints plus the harness that reproduces the paper's evaluation. The CMA-ES merge search itself is not in this repo.
architecture: Evaluation-only codebase: the tree is evaluate.py plus evomerge/{eval,models,modules} — no search code. A GitHub code search for `cma` across the repo returns 0 hits; README states it "serves as a central hub ... includes models and code for reproducing the evaluation presented in our paper." The merge optimizer lives in the paper, which the card's context below draws from.

The evolved space, per arXiv 2403.13187: (a) parameter space — DARE-TIES sparsification plus per-layer weight-mixing coefficients (one config per embedding/transformer block), optimized by Optuna's CMA-ES with all initial values 0.5, sigma 1/6, population 4+⌊3·ln(n_params)⌋, 1000 trials, fitness = accuracy on 1069 held-out Japanese GSM8k items; (b) data-flow space — an indicator array I over M=64 layers repeated r=3 times (so T=192 slots) plus a scaling matrix W, optimized by EvoJAX CMA-ES for 100 generations, population 128, with W forced to 1 on same-model adjacent hops so any gain comes from layer stacking/permutation alone.

Config-driven runner: each YAML pairs a model with one or more evaluators. Models are evomerge.CausalLMWithvLLM (vLLM backend, default template ja-alpaca-cot, stop tokens Instruction:/Response:) or evomerge.LLaVA for the VLM; evaluate.py loads the config, set_seed(42), instantiates, runs evaluator(model), and writes results/<config-basename>.json.

Three evaluators ship in-tree: JaMGSM (juletxara/mgsm, ja test split), JaVGVQA (SakanaAI/JA-VG-VQA-500) and JaVLMBenchIntheWild (SakanaAI/JA-VLM-Bench-In-the-Wild). MGSM-JA is zero-shot pass@1 accuracy on the last number regex-extracted from the response; every evaluator also reports a `_ja` strict variant that calls fasttext on lid.176.ftz and zeroes answers not labeled Japanese with p>0.5. VLM scoring is MeCab-tokenized ROUGE-L after neologdn full/half-width normalization.
advantages: The released weights are the artifact: EvoLLM-JP-v1-7B scores 52.0 MGSM-JA and 70.5 on lm-eval-harness JP average where its source models sit at or below 30.0 and 66.1; EvoLLM-JP-v1-10B reaches 55.6/66.2 and EvoLLM-JP-A-v1-7B 52.4/69.0. Weight-level capability gain with zero gradient steps — the cleanest demonstration in the catalog that recombination is a distinct improvement operator.

The harness encodes the exact protocol behind those claims, not a leaderboard snapshot: the fasttext Japanese-answer gate, the last-number extraction heuristic (needed because source models use incompatible output formats), and MeCab-tokenized ROUGE for VQA are all visible and re-runnable.

EvoLLM-JP-v1-10B is produced by merging EvoLLM-JP-v1-7B with shisa-gamma-7b-v1 — a merge of a merge — and EvoVLM-JP crosses modality (LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B + shisa-gamma-7b-v1), so the released set doubles as a worked example of iterated and cross-domain recombination.
